title: Marcus Aurelius
text:
Marcus Aurelius was born on April 26, 121 AD, in Rome, to Marcus Annius Verus and Domitia Calvilla. His family was of Italic origin and had a strong connection to the Roman aristocracy. After his father's death when Marcus was three years old, he was raised by his mother and paternal grandfather, Marcus Annius Verus. He was educated at home, studying Greek and Latin, and developed a passion for philosophy, particularly Stoicism. His early life was marked by a strong sense of discipline and self-control, which would serve him well in his later years.

As a young man, Marcus displayed enthusiasm for wrestling and boxing, and he trained in wrestling and learned to fight in armor. He was also interested in philosophy and was encouraged by his teacher, Diognetus, to pursue a life of philosophical study. At the age of 12, Marcus took up the dress and habits of a philosopher, studying while wearing a rough Greek cloak and sleeping on the ground. He was educated by several tutors, including Herodes Atticus and Marcus Cornelius Fronto, who helped him develop his writing and oratory skills.

In 138 AD, Hadrian, the Roman Emperor, adopted Marcus as his son and heir to the throne. As part of this adoption, Marcus was betrothed to Faustina, the daughter of Antoninus Pius, who would later become his wife. Marcus became M. Aelius Aurelius Verus and began to take on more responsibilities as the heir apparent. He served as consul in 140, 145, and 161 AD, and was appointed as a sevir, one of the knights' six commanders.

When Antoninus Pius died in 161 AD, Marcus acceded to the throne alongside his adoptive brother, Lucius Aurelius Verus. As emperor, Marcus faced numerous challenges, including a series of military conflicts, including the Parthian War and the Marcomannic Wars. He also had to deal with the Antonine Plague, which devastated the population of the Roman Empire, causing the deaths of five to ten million people. Despite these challenges, Marcus remained committed to his philosophical principles, writing Meditations, a work that would become a cornerstone of Stoic philosophy.

Marcus Aurelius was a prolific writer and philosopher, and his work Meditations is one of the most important sources for understanding ancient Stoic philosophy. He was known for his wisdom, justice, and moderation, and his reign is often referred to as the "Golden Age" of the Roman Empire. Throughout his life, Marcus was guided by a strong sense of duty and a commitment to living in accordance with his philosophical principles. He died on March 17, 180 AD, at the age of 58, leaving behind a legacy as one of the greatest emperors in Roman history.

The sources for Marcus Aurelius' life are varied and include the Historia Augusta, a collection of biographies written in the 4th century AD, as well as the writings of Cassius Dio, a Greek senator who wrote a history of Rome. Additionally, Marcus' own writings, including Meditations, provide valuable insights into his thoughts and experiences as emperor and philosopher. Despite the challenges of reconstructing his life from these sources, it is clear that Marcus Aurelius was a remarkable individual who left a lasting impact on Western philosophy and politics.

title: Winston Churchill
text:
Winston Churchill was a British statesman, military officer, and writer who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and again from 1951 to 1955. He was born on November 30, 1874, at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, England, to a wealthy and aristocratic family. His father, Lord Randolph Churchill, was a member of parliament and a descendant of the Dukes of Marlborough. His mother, Jennie Jerome, was an American, and Churchill's mixed parentage would influence his views and career.

Churchill was educated at Harrow School and the Royal Military College at Sandhurst. He joined the British Army in 1895 and served in British India, the Mahdist War, and the Second Boer War. During his time in the army, he began writing and sent reports to the Daily Graphic in London. He became a war correspondent and wrote books about his campaigns, including "The Story of the Malakand Field Force" and "The River War".

In 1900, Churchill was elected a Conservative member of parliament for Oldham. However, he soon became disillusioned with the Conservative Party's protectionist policies and defected to the Liberal Party in 1904. As a Liberal, he became a vocal critic of the Conservative government and a supporter of free trade and social reform. He was appointed Under-Secretary of State for the Colonial Office in 1905 and worked to implement the government's policies in the colonies.

Churchill's early years in politics were marked by his radical views and his advocacy for social reform. He championed prison reform and workers' social security, and he was a strong supporter of women's suffrage. However, his views were not without controversy, and he was criticized for his handling of the Tonypandy Riots in 1911.

In 1911, Churchill was appointed Home Secretary, a position that gave him responsibility for law and order. He implemented several reforms, including the establishment of a probation service and the improvement of prison conditions. However, his time as Home Secretary was cut short when he was appointed First Lord of the Admiralty in 1911. He played a key role in the development of the British naval fleet, but his plans were disrupted by the outbreak of World War I.

During World War I, Churchill served as First Lord of the Admiralty, but the disastrous Gallipoli campaign led to his demotion to Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. He resigned in 1915 and joined the Royal Scots Fusiliers on the Western Front for six months. He later served as Minister of Munitions, Secretary of State for War, and Secretary of State for the Colonies.

In the 1920s, Churchill was Chancellor of the Exchequer, but his decision to return sterling to the gold standard in 1925 was criticized for depressing the UK economy. He was out of government for several years, during which time he wrote several books, including a biography of his father and a history of the English-speaking peoples.

In the 1930s, Churchill became a vocal critic of Nazi Germany and a strong advocate for rearmament. He warned of the dangers of German militarism and advocated for a strong British defense policy. When World War II broke out in 1939, Churchill was appointed First Lord of the Admiralty once again. He became Prime Minister in May 1940, after the resignation of Neville Chamberlain, and led the British government through the rest of the war.

As Prime Minister, Churchill played a key role in the Allied victory, rallying the British people with his speeches and writings. He formed a national government and worked closely with the United States and other allies to defeat Nazi Germany. He also played a key role in the development of the Atlantic Charter, which outlined the Allied goals for the post-war world.

After the war, Churchill lost the 1945 general election, but he continued to serve as Leader of the Opposition. He became Prime Minister again in 1951 and served until 1955, when he retired due to ill health. During his second term, he focused on foreign policy, including Anglo-American relations and the preservation of the British Empire.

Churchill was a prolific writer and was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. He died on January 24, 1965, and was given a state funeral. He remains one of the most significant figures of the 20th century, known for his leadership during World War II and his contributions to literature and politics.

Churchill's legacy is complex and multifaceted. He is remembered as a great wartime leader who played a key role in the Allied victory. However, he is also criticized for his role in the Bengal famine, his views on colonialism, and his handling of the Greek Civil War. Despite these criticisms, Churchill remains a popular figure in the UK and the rest of the Anglosphere, and his influence can still be seen in British politics today.

title: Sun Wenguang
text:
Sun Wenguang was a prominent Chinese activist and vocal critic of the Chinese government, born on August 26, 1934, in Rongcheng City. His father was a naval officer of the National Government, and Sun himself joined the Navy at a young age. He later went on to become a professor of Physics at Shandong University in Jinan, a position he held from 1982 until his retirement in 1994.

Sun had a history of speaking out against the Chinese government, which led to him being one of the original signatories of Charter 08, a document calling for human rights and democratic reforms. His activism did not go unnoticed, and he faced harassment due to his associations with critics of the Communist Party of China.

On April 5, 2009, Sun was severely beaten by a group of men while visiting the grave of former Chinese Premier Zhao Ziyang at Heroes' Mountain in Jinan. The attack left him with three broken ribs and injuries to his spine, head, back, arms, and legs, requiring hospitalization. This incident was not an isolated event, as Sun continued to face pressure from the authorities.

In 2010, Sun's application for a passport was rejected, just before the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony for Liu Xiaobo, a prominent Chinese dissident. This rejection seemed to be a deliberate attempt to prevent Sun from traveling abroad.

On August 1, 2018, Sun was giving an interview to Voice of America when Chinese security forces entered his home and seized him. Two Voice of America journalists, Feng Yibing and Allen Ai, were also detained for several hours while trying to reach Sun. This incident highlighted the continued pressure Sun faced from the Chinese authorities.

In 2022, reports emerged that Sun may have died in 2021 at the age of 87. However, the Chinese authorities have refused to confirm or deny these reports, leaving Sun's fate uncertain. Despite this, Sun's writings continue to be published, with several books released in Hong Kong, including "Against the Wind for 33 Years: Dictatorship after 1977 versus Constitutional Democracy" and "A Country in a Century of Trouble: From Mao Zedong to Jiang Zemin". His writings offer a glimpse into his thoughts on the Chinese government, democracy, and human rights.

title: Phil Vickery (rugby union)
text:
Philip John Vickery, known as "The Raging Bull," is an English former rugby union player born on March 14, 1976, in Barnstaple, Devon, England, to Cornish parents. He developed an interest in sports at a young age and started playing rugby at 12. By 16, he gained his first National Representative honour, being picked for the England Schools U16s group. Vickery left school at 16 to work as a herdsman on his parents' farm and later joined the Cornish club Bude, then moved to Redruth, where he first appeared in an England Colts side.

In 1995, Vickery joined Gloucester Rugby, where he spent 11 years and became known for his impressive rugby skills. During his time at Gloucester, he started in the 2002 Zurich Championship Final and won several honors, including a Powergen Cup Final. Vickery's representative career with England began in 1998 when he made his debut against Wales at 21. He went on to earn 73 international caps, including a World Cup-winning squad in 2003, where he played in all seven matches.

Vickery's rugby career was marked by several notable achievements, including touring Australia and South Africa with the British & Irish Lions and captaining the England squad in the 2007 Rugby World Cup. He also played in three Rugby World Cups and was part of the England team that won the 2003 World Cup. In 2006, Vickery joined London Wasps, where he won the Heineken Cup and the 2008 Guinness Premiership title.

However, Vickery's career was cut short due to several neck injuries, which forced him to retire from rugby in 2010. He played his last game at Kingsholm against Gloucester, where he started his career. After his retirement, Vickery went on to become a co-commentator for ITV's coverage of the 2011 Rugby World Cup and won the 2011 series of Celebrity Masterchef.

Vickery has also been involved in various charitable and community activities. He was appointed a Deputy Lieutenant of Gloucestershire in 2015 and has a range of clothing named after him. Vickery is also a qualified cattle inseminator and has tattoos on his left and right shoulders. Throughout his career, Vickery demonstrated his passion and dedication to rugby, earning him the nickname "The Raging Bull." His achievements on and off the pitch have made him a respected figure in the rugby world.

title: Jeff Beukeboom
text:
Jeff Beukeboom is a Canadian professional ice hockey coach and former player who played in the National Hockey League (NHL) from 1986 to 1999. Born on March 28, 1965, in Ajax, Ontario, Beukeboom grew up in Lindsay, Ontario. He played junior hockey for the Sault Ste. Marie Greyhounds from 1982 to 1985 before being selected by the Edmonton Oilers in the first round of the 1983 NHL Entry Draft.

Beukeboom played for the Edmonton Oilers and New York Rangers, winning four Stanley Cup championships in 1987, 1988, 1990, and 1994. He was known for his hard-hitting defensive play and was a key member of the Rangers' top defensive pairing with Brian Leetch. Beukeboom's stay-at-home play allowed Leetch to lead the rush and kept opposing players out of the goal crease. He led the Rangers in penalty minutes three times and was an alternate captain for the team.

During his playing career, Beukeboom was also known for his philanthropic efforts, particularly with Ice Hockey in Harlem. He won the Rangers' Crumb Bum Award in 1996 for his service to local youngsters. Beukeboom appeared in a memorable This is Sportscenter spot in which he assaulted ESPN's Steve Levy after being told Levy had referred to Beukeboom as "Puke-a-boom."

Beukeboom's playing career was cut short due to multiple concussions, the most devastating of which came from a sucker punch by Matt Johnson of the Los Angeles Kings in November 1998. He was diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome and ordered to never play hockey again. Beukeboom officially retired in July 1999 with 1,890 NHL penalty minutes in 804 games played. He is currently second all-time on the Rangers' penalty minutes list.

After retiring from hockey, Beukeboom went on to become a coach. He returned to hockey as an assistant coach for the Toronto Roadrunners in the American Hockey League (AHL) for the 2003-04 season. In 2005, he became the president and part-owner of the Lindsay Muskies of the Ontario Provincial Junior "A" Hockey League. Beukeboom also worked as an assistant coach for the Barrie Colts of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) and the Sudbury Wolves.

In 2012, Beukeboom joined the Connecticut Whale, then known as the Hartford Wolf Pack, as an assistant coach. Four years later, he was hired as an assistant coach for the New York Rangers. Beukeboom is also a family man, with a son, Brock, who played for the UPEI Panthers and was drafted by the Tampa Bay Lightning. His daughter, Tyson, played college rugby for St. Francis Xavier University and was named the CIS Female Athlete of the Year in 2012.

Throughout his career, Beukeboom has been recognized for his achievements, including being named to the OHL All-Star First Team in 1984-85 and being ranked No. 50 all-time of the 901 New York Rangers who had played during the team's first 82 seasons in the 2009 book 100 Ranger Greats.

title: León Dujovne
text:
León Dujovne was a prominent Argentine writer, philosopher, essayist, and journalist, born on November 15, 1898, in the village of Kurilovich, near Mohyliv-Podilskyi, in the Russian Empire, to Jewish parents. When he was just one year old, his family emigrated to Argentina, settling in Basavilbaso, Entre Ríos, one of the Jewish colonies established by Baron Maurice de Hirsch in the province. This early exposure to a diverse cultural environment likely influenced his future work.

Dujovne went on to lead a distinguished academic and literary career, producing notable works that showcased his expertise in philosophy and Jewish culture. One of his most significant contributions is the four-volume work "Spinoza. Su vida, su época, su obra, su influencia," published between 1941 and 1945 by the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters at the University of Buenos Aires. This comprehensive study explores the life, era, work, and influence of the renowned philosopher Baruch Spinoza.

In addition to his work on Spinoza, Dujovne also wrote "El judaísmo como cultura," published in 1980 by Ediciones Nueva Presencia in Buenos Aires. This book is a testament to his interest in Jewish culture and its significance in the modern world. Furthermore, he translated Maimonides' "The Guide for the Perplexed" from the French version by Salomon Munk, publishing it in three volumes in Buenos Aires in 1955. A revised edition of this translation, complete with an introduction and notes by Angelina Muñiz-Huberman, was published in Mexico City in 2001.

Throughout his life, Dujovne's work demonstrated a deep understanding of Jewish philosophy and culture, as well as a commitment to exploring and sharing knowledge with a broader audience. His writing continues to be an important part of his legacy, offering insights into the intersections of philosophy, culture, and identity. Dujovne passed away on January 16, 1984, leaving behind a lasting impact on the world of philosophy and literature.

title: Karyn Pugliese
text:
Karyn Pugliese is a highly respected investigative journalist who has made significant contributions to Canadian journalism and press freedom. As a citizen of the Algonquins of Pikwàkanagàn First Nation in Ontario and a status Indian under Canada's Indian Act, Pugliese has used her platform to advocate for Indigenous rights and representation in the media. Her impressive career has taken her to various news organizations, including the Aboriginal Peoples Television Network (APTN), CBC, and ichannel.

Pugliese's early life and education laid the foundation for her future success. Born and raised in Ottawa, Ontario, she frequently visited Pikwàkanagàn in her youth and developed a strong connection to her Indigenous heritage. Pugliese graduated from the Ottawa Alternative High School program and went on to earn a combined honours degree in Journalism and History from Carleton University in 1998. She later earned a master's degree in history from Carleton University in 2006, with a thesis titled "So, where are you from?" Glimpsing the history of Ottawa-Gatineau's urban Indian communities.

Pugliese's career in journalism spans over two decades, with her first job as a parliamentary correspondent for APTN in 2000. She credits APTN's daycare policy and flexible hours for allowing her to balance her work and family life as a single mother. Her son, Zackery Liberty, is a guitarist with the indie rock group Farewell Davidson. Pugliese has worked in various roles, including as a reporter for CTV and CBC, and as a communications officer for the Assembly of First Nations.

One of Pugliese's most notable roles was as the host and producer of ichannel's #FAQMP, a current affairs program that allowed viewers to submit questions for Members of Parliament. The show was praised for its innovative approach to democracy and its hyper-local focus. During her time at APTN, Pugliese led the news department as the executive director of News and Current Affairs, overseeing the creation of new programming such as Nation to Nation and InFocus.

Pugliese has received numerous awards and honours for her work, including two Charles Bury Awards from the Canadian Association of Journalists, the Gordon Sinclair Award for distinguished achievement in journalism, and the Hyman Solomon Award for Public Policy Journalism. She was also chosen as the twenty-fifth Martin Wise Goodman Canadian Nieman Fellow at Harvard University, graduating in 2020.

In addition to her work as a journalist, Pugliese has been a vocal advocate for press freedom and Indigenous representation in the media. She has served as the president of the Canadian Association of Journalists and has sat on the board of Canadian Journalists for Free Expression. Pugliese has also worked with Journalist for Human Rights, training young Indigenous journalists and advocating for human rights.

Throughout her career, Pugliese has intervened in over three Supreme Court cases, fighting for press freedom and the rights of journalists. Her contributions to Canadian journalism have been significant, and her commitment to Indigenous representation and advocacy has made a lasting impact on the industry. Pugliese's achievements serve as an inspiration to aspiring journalists and a testament to the importance of diverse voices in the media. As a respected leader in Canadian journalism, Pugliese continues to make a difference through her work, using her platform to amplify Indigenous voices and promote press freedom.

title: Ingo Titze
text:
Ingo R. Titze is a renowned voice scientist who has made significant contributions to the field of vocal science and vocology. He is currently the executive director of the National Center for Voice and Speech and an adjunct professor in the Department of Otolaryngology/Head and Neck Surgery at the University of Utah. Additionally, he holds a distinguished professorship at the Department of Communication Sciences and Disorders at the University of Iowa.

Titze's educational background includes a Bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Utah, followed by a Master's degree in electrical engineering with a minor in physics from the same institution. He then earned his Ph.D. in physics from Brigham Young University in 1972. Throughout his career, Titze has held various positions at prestigious institutions, including the University of Utah, University of Iowa, Gallaudet University, and the Denver Center for the Performing Arts.

One of Titze's most notable contributions to the field of vocal science is the development of the discipline of vocology, which is the study of the science and practice of voice habilitation. He coined the term "vocology" and proposed it as a discipline parallel to audiology. Titze has also developed several university courses, including principles of voice production, acoustics, biomechanics of speech, and vocal pedagogy.

Titze's research has focused on voice health and voice disorders, and he has been awarded multiple grants from the National Institutes of Health to study these topics. His research has been prolific, with over 160 research articles listed at the NIH. He has also written several books on the human voice, including "Fascinations with the Human Voice," "Vocology: The Science and Practice of Voice Habilitation," and "Principles of Voice Production."

Throughout his career, Titze has received numerous awards and honors for his contributions to the field of vocal science. These include the Kay-Pentax Lecturer and Awards, Honors of the Association from the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, and the Science Writing Award for Professional in Acoustics from The Acoustical Society of America. He has also been featured in various media outlets, including BBC Radio 3, Reuters, and CNN.

In addition to his research and teaching, Titze is also involved in the Summer Vocology Institute, which is housed at the University of Utah. He has also been a consultant to the Department of Linguistics/Speech Analysis at Bell Laboratories and a visiting lecturer at the Department of Hearing/Speech Science at the University of Maryland.

Overall, Ingo R. Titze is a highly respected figure in the field of vocal science, with a career spanning multiple institutions and a wide range of contributions to research, teaching, and service. His work has had a significant impact on our understanding of the human voice and has helped to establish vocology as a distinct discipline.

title: Jennifer Sevilla
text:

In the 2000s, Sevilla appeared in films like "Kung Ako Na Lang Sana" (2003) with Sharon Cuneta and Aga Muhlach, and "Paraiso: Tatlong Kwento Ng Pag-asa" (2007) with Maricel Soriano.

Throughout her career, Sevilla has received several award nominations, including multiple FAMAS and Gawad Urian Award nominations for Best Supporting Actress. Her notable nominations include Best Supporting Actress for "Kahapon, May Dalawang Bata" (1999) at the FAMAS Awards and the Gawad Urian Awards.

Sevilla's extensive filmography spans over four decades, with over 50 films and numerous television appearances to her credit. Her television credits include "That's Entertainment," "Lovingly Yours," "Young Love Sweet Love," and "Maalaala Mo Kaya," among others. She has also appeared in recent TV shows such as "Ang Probinsyano" (2021) and "Teen Clash" (2023).

In addition to her acting career, Sevilla has also been part of various projects, including commercials and public service announcements. Her dedication to her craft has made her a respected figure in the Philippine entertainment industry.

Overall, Jennifer Sevilla has established herself as a talented and versatile actress, with a career spanning over 40 years in film and television. Her contributions to the industry have been recognized through numerous award nominations, solidifying her place as one of the most accomplished actresses in the Philippines.

title: Will Keane
text:
Will Keane is a professional footballer who plays as a forward or attacking midfielder for Preston North End and the Republic of Ireland national team. Born on January 11, 1993, in Stockport, Greater Manchester, Keane began his career with Manchester United, joining the club's academy at the age of 11. He worked his way up through the academy, making his first appearance for the under-18s at 14 and scoring 13 goals in 26 appearances in the 2009-10 season.

Keane's performances earned him a three-year scholarship with Manchester United, and he made his senior debut in 2011 against Blackburn Rovers. However, his career was hampered by injuries, including a knee ligament injury that kept him out for the entire 2012-13 season. Despite making 17 appearances for Manchester United's first team, Keane had loan spells with Wigan Athletic, Queens Park Rangers, Sheffield Wednesday, and Preston North End.

In 2016, Keane made a permanent move to Hull City, where he made 84 appearances and scored 13 goals over three seasons. He had a loan spell at Ipswich Town in 2019 before being released by Hull City at the end of the 2018-19 season. Keane then joined Ipswich Town permanently on a one-year deal and made 29 appearances, scoring six goals.

In October 2020, Keane joined Wigan Athletic on a short-term contract and scored five goals in 12 appearances. He signed a new two-year deal with Wigan in June 2021 and went on to finish as top goalscorer in the 2021-22 season with 26 goals. Keane's impressive form earned him the EFL League One Golden Boot and a place in the PFA Team of the Year.

In September 2021, Keane was called up to the Republic of Ireland squad for the first time, having declared his interest in playing for Ireland in 2019. He made his debut for Ireland in a World Cup qualifier against Portugal in November 2021. Keane qualified for Ireland through his father and has since become a regular member of the squad.

In July 2023, Keane joined Preston North End for an undisclosed fee and became the club's top scorer in the 2023-24 season with 13 goals. His contract was extended until 2026 after the end of that season. Throughout his career, Keane has won several honors, including the FA Youth Cup with Manchester United and the EFL League One title with Wigan Athletic.

title: Settimo Mineo
text:
Settimo Mineo, also known as "Tonton Settimo", is an Italian member of the Sicilian Mafia's Pagliarelli mandamento from Palermo. Born on November 28, 1938, in Palermo, Mineo officially owns a jewelry shop in the city, but is widely regarded as the oldest boss of the Sicilian Mafia. His life has been marked by violence and loss, including the murder of his brother Antonino in 1981 and an ambush in 1982 that killed his brother Giuseppe.

Mineo's involvement with the Mafia has led to several run-ins with the law. In the 1980s, he was testified against by pentito Tommaso Buscetta, resulting in a five-year prison sentence in the Maxi Trial. After his release, he was re-arrested in 2006 and sentenced in the "Gotha" trial, but was released in 2013 by decision of the Supreme Court of Cassation.

Despite being a former associate of Antonio Rotolo, a historical ally of the Corleonesi Mafia clan, Mineo has formed alliances with rival clans in recent years. He has aligned himself with the Inzerillo Mafia clan, and had Salvatore Sorrentino as his right-hand man. This shift in allegiances demonstrates Mineo's adaptability and willingness to form strategic alliances within the Cosa Nostra.

In 2018, Mineo was elected as the new head of the Sicilian Mafia Commission following the death of Salvatore Riina. However, his tenure was short-lived, as he was re-arrested on December 4, 2018, in the operation "Cupola 2.0" conducted by the Carabinieri. He was charged with being the new head of the "Dome" of Cosa Nostra.

According to investigators, Mineo's arrest led to Giuseppe Calvaruso taking over as the new head of the Pagliarelli mandamento. Calvaruso is known for his modern approach to managing the mandamento, and was reportedly one of Mineo's most trusted men.

In his personal life, Mineo is known for his charisma and mediation skills. He is a devout Catholic and, along with his wife, attended mass regularly at the Church of San Giovanni Decollato in Ballarò, Palermo. For a year, they even participated in a volunteer project at the church, which involved an after-school program for children. Despite his involvement in organized crime, Mineo appears to have maintained a level of anonymity, avoiding the use of mobile phones and often moving on foot to visit other Mafia bosses.

title: Sayaka Ando
text:
Sayaka Ando is a Japanese gravure idol and fashion model born on May 24, 1981, in Takasaki, Gunma, and raised in Sendai, Japan. title: Pablo Ganet
text:
Pablo Ganet Comitre is a professional footballer who plays as a midfielder for Indonesian Super League club Persita Tangerang. He was born on November 4, 1994, in Málaga, Andalusia, Spain. Throughout his career, Ganet has demonstrated his skills as a midfielder, playing for various teams in Spain and abroad. His move to Persita Tangerang in 2025 marked a new chapter in his career, as he continues to play in the Indonesian Super League. With his international experience and skills, Ganet remains a valuable player for both his club and national team.

Ganet's career statistics are recorded up to January 22, 2024, and he has a profile on various football websites, including National-Football-Teams.com and Soccerway. His achievements include winning the Botola with Ittihad Tanger in the 2017-2018 season. As a player of Bubi descent, Ganet continues to make a name for himself in the world of football.

title: Yuu Watase
text:
Yuu Watase is a renowned Japanese manga artist born on March 5, 1970, in Kishiwada, Osaka. With a career spanning over three decades, Watase has published more than 50 volumes of one-shots and long-running manga series, showcasing her versatility and creativity in the manga industry. Her journey as a manga artist began at a young age, and she debuted in 1989 with the short story "Pajama de Ojama" at the age of 18.

Watase's early life and education played a significant role in shaping her career. Although she did not receive formal training in manga drawing until after high school, she was naturally inclined towards art. She attended a private art school, where she learned the basics of manga drawing, but left midway as her first short story had already been published.

One of Watase's most notable works is the popular manga series "Fushigi Yûgi," which has been published for many years and has gained a significant following. Another notable work is "Ceres, Celestial Legend," which earned her the 43rd Shogakukan Manga Award in the shōjo category in 1998. In 2008, Watase began her first shōnen serialization, "Arata: The Legend," which further showcased her range as a manga artist.

Watase's approach to her work is rooted in traditional methods, which she believes allow her to infuse her art with more feelings. While she is accustomed to working with colored inks and markers, she has also experimented with digital programs like Adobe Photoshop to enhance her traditional work. However, her experiences with digital media have been limited, and she has expressed a desire to explore new media further.

Despite her success, Watase has faced challenges in her career, particularly with regards to her work on "Arata: The Legend." In a 2014 blog post, she shared her struggles with an editor who consistently asked her to redraw scenes, leading to burnout and a loss of interest in the manga. Watase's experience highlights the pressures and demands that manga artists often face.

In addition to her professional life, Watase has been open about her personal life, including her identity. In 2019, she came out as X-gender, a Japanese non-binary gender identity. Following her announcement, an editor for Viz Media's Shojo Beat imprint clarified that Watase's pronouns in English are still "she" and "her."

Throughout her career, Watase has created a wide range of works, including "Shishunki Miman Okotowari," "Epotoransu! Mai," "Alice 19th," and "Absolute Boyfriend." Her manga has been published in various formats, including Flower Comics, Shōnen Sunday Comics, and Watase Yuu Masterpiece Collection. Her works have been well-received by fans and critics alike, and she continues to be a prominent figure in the manga industry.

Watase's contributions to the manga industry have been significant, and her dedication to her craft is evident in her work. With a career spanning over three decades, she has established herself as a talented and versatile manga artist. Her experiences, both personal and professional, have shaped her approach to her work and continue to influence her creations. As she continues to work on new projects, fans and readers can look forward to seeing more of her remarkable work.

title: Chris Woakes
text:
Chris Woakes is an English cricketer who plays internationally for England in all formats and domestically represents Warwickshire. He was born on March 2, 1989, in Birmingham, and attended Barr Beacon Language College in Walsall. Woakes began playing cricket at the age of seven with Aston Manor Cricket Club, before moving to Walmley Cricket Club. He also played for Herefordshire County Cricket Club in the 2006 Minor Counties Trophy.

Woakes' cricket career began to take shape when he played for Warwickshire's under-15, under-17, academy, and Second XI teams between 2004 and 2007. He made his debut for the Warwickshire First XI in 2006, taking three wickets in one match. In 2008, he became a regular for the Warwickshire First XI, taking 42 wickets at an average of 20.57 runs per wicket in the County Championship season.

In 2009, Woakes was called up to the England Lions squad and made his Lions debut against the West Indies, taking 6/43 in the first innings. He also scored his maiden first-class century, 131 not out, against Hampshire. Woakes made his One Day International (ODI) and Twenty20 International (T20I) debuts for England in 2011, and his Test debut in 2013.

Woakes has played for several teams in the Indian Premier League (IPL), including Kolkata Knight Riders, Royal Challengers Bangalore, and Delhi Capitals. He was bought by Kolkata Knight Riders in the 2017 IPL auction and took 17 wickets in 13 matches. He played for Royal Challengers Bangalore in 2018, taking eight wickets in five matches. In 2020, he was bought by Delhi Capitals but pulled out of the tournament to keep himself fresh for England's Test season.

Woakes has had a successful international career, playing for England in all formats. He was part of the England teams that won the 2019 Cricket World Cup and the 2022 T20 World Cup. He has taken over 150 ODI wickets and 100 Test wickets, and has scored several crucial runs for England. In 2019, he was named in England's squad for the Cricket World Cup, and took three wickets in the semi-final against Australia. He also took three wickets in the final against New Zealand, helping England win the tournament.

In addition to his cricket career, Woakes is an avid supporter of local football club Aston Villa F.C. and was a trainee footballer with Walsall F.C. as a winger until the age of 14. Woakes has continued to play for England in all formats, and has been named in several squads, including the 2021 ICC Men's T20 World Cup and the 2022 ICC Men's T20 World Cup. He was part of the England team that won the 2022 T20 World Cup, beating Pakistan in the final. In 2023, Woakes was recalled to the England team for the 3rd Test of the Ashes series, where he took three wickets in each innings and finished 32 not out in the second innings, hitting the winning runs. His performances in the series earned him the award for England's player of the series.

title: Diosdado Cabello
text:
Diosdado Cabello Rondón is a Venezuelan politician who has held various positions in the government, including Minister of Interior, Justice and Peace since 2024. He was born on April 15, 1963, in El Furrial, Monagas state, and graduated from the Venezuelan Military Academy in 1987, where he was ranked second in his class. Cabello's background is in engineering, with undergraduate and graduate degrees from the Instituto Universitario Politécnico de las Fuerzas Armadas Nacionales and the Andrés Bello Catholic University, respectively.

Cabello's political career began when he befriended Hugo Chávez while at the military academy, and he played a key role in Chávez's return to power following the 2002 Venezuelan coup d'état attempt. He became a leading member of Chávez's Movimiento V República (MVR) and remained a prominent figure in the ruling United Socialist Party of Venezuela (PSUV) after MVR was merged into the party in 2007. Cabello has held various positions in the government, including head of the national telecommunications commission (CONATEL), chief of staff to Chávez, and Vice President of Venezuela.

In 2004, Cabello was elected governor of Miranda state, a position he held until 2008. He lost the 2008 election to Henrique Capriles Radonski and was subsequently appointed Public Works and Housing Minister. Cabello has also served as the head of CONATEL, where he intervened in the operations of 32 radio and 2 television stations, a decision that was criticized as an act of censorship.

In 2010, Cabello was elected to the National Assembly, where he served as president from 2012 to 2016. During his tenure, he was accused of intimidating opponents and using his program, "Con el Mazo Dando," to make accusations against them. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) has expressed concerns about the program's impact on freedom of expression and the intimidation of critics.

Cabello has been accused of various forms of corruption, including drug trafficking and nepotism. In 2013, there were at least 17 formal corruption allegations lodged against him in Venezuela's prosecutors office. The US Department of State has offered a $10 million reward for information leading to his arrest and/or conviction on charges of drug trafficking and narco-terrorism.

In addition to his government positions, Cabello has been involved in various controversies. He has been sanctioned by several countries, including the United States, Canada, the European Union, Switzerland, Mexico, and Panama, for his alleged involvement in human rights abuses and corruption. In 2020, Cabello tested positive for COVID-19 during the pandemic in Venezuela.

Cabello's influence in the Venezuelan government has been described as significant, with many considering him the second most powerful man in the country. His network of patronage and corruption has been compared to that of a "mafia-like" organization. Despite these controversies, Cabello remains a prominent figure in Venezuelan politics.

Cabello's personal life has also been subject to scrutiny. His wife, Marleny Contreras, was a member of the National Assembly until she became minister of tourism in 2015. His sister, Glenna, is a political scientist and has worked for the Venezuelan Permanent Mission to the United Nations. His brother, José David, is the head of SENIAT, Venezuela's revenue service.

Overall, Diosdado Cabello's career has been marked by controversy and allegations of corruption. Despite his influential position in the Venezuelan government, he has been accused of various forms of corruption and has been sanctioned by several countries. His role in the government has been the subject of criticism and scrutiny, both domestically and internationally.

title: Dana Awartani
text:
Dana Awartani is a Saudi visual artist of Palestinian ethnicity, born in 1987 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, where she currently resides. She is known for her work in various mediums, including painting, video art, and sand mosaic, which often incorporate traditional methods of Islamic art. Awartani's artistic journey began with her education, where she earned a Foundation Degree in Art and Design from the Byam Shaw School of Art in 2006. She then went on to pursue a bachelor's degree in fine art from Central Saint Martins in London, which she completed in 2009.

Awartani furthered her education by earning a master's degree in traditional arts from The Prince's School in London in 2011. During her time at The Prince's School, she learned various traditional techniques from cultures around the world, including stained glass, miniature painting, and gilding. However, she was unable to study the traditional illumination of texts, so she found an instructor in Turkey to master this discipline. This diverse educational background has had a significant impact on Awartani's work, which seeks to incorporate traditional Islamic art methods into a contemporary context.

Awartani's artwork is characterized by its use of geometric patterning and intricate details, often integrating traditional Islamic art styles. Her work explores the relationship between geometry and nature, as well as how truths can be translated through art using geometric principles. She visualizes a sacred language through a symbolic and multi-layered aesthetic, using methods that have been passed down for over 1,000 years. Awartani's artistic process is a sacred spiritual practice that she uses as a way to worship God and for God, teaching her patience and respect.

In her own words, Awartani views Islamic art as a way to connect with her heritage and culture. She notes that as Arabs, they are often surrounded by fine art, but may not be aware of it. Awartani's work seeks to change this by highlighting the beauty and significance of Islamic art. Her artwork has been recognized internationally, including her inclusion in the Rhizoma project of the 55th Venice Biennale in 2013. Her work is also part of the collections of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington D.C. and the British Museum in London.

Awartani's unique blend of traditional and contemporary art has made her a notable figure in the art world. Her work continues to inspire and educate others about the beauty and significance of Islamic art. Through her art, Awartani aims to share her passion for Islamic art and to showcase its relevance in the modern world. By doing so, she hopes to promote a greater understanding and appreciation of Islamic art and culture. Overall, Dana Awartani's work is a testament to the power of art to transcend boundaries and to connect people across cultures and traditions.

title: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
text:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah was a prominent barrister, politician, and the founder of Pakistan. Born on December 25, 1876, in Karachi, British India, Jinnah was trained as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn in London. Upon his return to India, he enrolled at the Bombay High Court and took an interest in national politics, which eventually replaced his legal practice. Jinnah rose to prominence in the Indian National Congress in the early 20th century, advocating for Hindu-Muslim unity and helping to shape the 1916 Lucknow Pact between the Congress and the All-India Muslim League.

Jinnah became a key leader in the All-India Home Rule League and proposed a fourteen-point constitutional reform plan to safeguard the political rights of Muslims in the Indian subcontinent. However, in 1920, he resigned from the Congress when it agreed to follow a campaign of satyagraha, which he regarded as political anarchy. Jinnah then joined the All-India Muslim League, working for the rights of Muslims in the subcontinent to protect them from marginalization in a Hindu-dominated state.

In 1940, the Muslim League, led by Jinnah, passed the Lahore Resolution, which called for a separate homeland for Muslims. During World War II, the League gained strength while Congress leaders were imprisoned, and in the provincial elections held after the war, it won most of the seats reserved for Muslims. The Congress and the Muslim League could not reach a power-sharing formula, leading to the independence of a Hindu-majority India and a predominantly Muslim state of Pakistan.

Jinnah served as the first governor-general of Pakistan, working to establish the government and policies to aid the millions of Muslim migrants who had emigrated from regions that became part of India to Pakistan. He personally supervised the establishment of refugee camps and worked tirelessly to build the new nation. Jinnah died on September 11, 1948, at the age of 71, just over a year after Pakistan gained independence.

Jinnah's early life was marked by his education in England, where he was influenced by 19th-century British liberalism and became an admirer of Western-style politics and culture. He abandoned local garb for Western-style clothing and became known for his impeccable dress sense. Jinnah's legal career was marked by his skilled handling of the 1908 "Caucus Case," which brought him great esteem. He was also a supporter of working-class causes and an active trade unionist, serving as President of the All India Postal Staff Union in 1925.

As a leader, Jinnah was known for his incredible faith in himself and his abilities. He was a clear thinker and a skilled orator, able to drive his points home with slow delivery and careful word choice. Jinnah's legacy in Pakistan is profound, with many regarding him as the Quaid-e-Azam ("Great Leader") and Baba-e-Qaum ("Father of the Nation"). His birthday is observed as a national holiday in Pakistan, and several universities and public buildings bear his name. According to his biographer, Stanley Wolpert, Jinnah remains Pakistan's greatest leader.

title: Brianna Keilar
text:
Brianna Keilar is an American journalist who has been working as a co-anchor of the afternoon edition of CNN News Central since April 2023. Born on September 21, 1980, in Canberra, Australia, Keilar is the daughter of an Australian father and an American mother. Her family moved to the United States when she was two years old and settled in Orange County, California. Keilar grew up in California and graduated from Mission Viejo High School in 1998, where she was voted homecoming queen. She then attended the University of California, Berkeley, graduating in 2001 with dual bachelor's degrees in mass communications and psychology.

Keilar began her career in journalism at a CBS affiliate in Yakima, Washington, where she worked as an anchor and reporter. She also co-hosted a morning drivetime show on a contemporary hits station. In 2002, Keilar joined CBS News, where she worked as an anchor, reporter, and producer for a CBS newscast that aired on MTVU. She also filled in as an anchor on the CBS News overnight newscast, Up to the Minute, and reported for the weekend edition of CBS Evening News.

In 2007, Keilar joined CNN as a correspondent for CNN Newsource, providing breaking news coverage and reports from Washington, D.C. for approximately 800 CNN Newsource partner stations. During her time at CNN, Keilar covered a wide range of stories, including the 2007 Virginia Tech massacre, where she was the first CNN correspondent at the scene. She also covered Congress, earning the 2009 National Press Foundation Everett McKinley Dirksen Award for Distinguished Reporting of Congress for her coverage of the $700 billion bank bailout.

Keilar's coverage of the Obama White House earned her the White House Correspondents' Association's 2014 Aldo Beckman Memorial Award. In 2019, Keilar began writing a column called Home Front, which tells stories of military families and tries to bridge the civilian-military divide. Keilar joined the CNN show New Day in 2021, co-anchoring with John Berman. She continued to work on the show until it was replaced by CNN This Morning in November 2022.

In her personal life, Keilar has been married twice. Her first marriage was to Dave French on May 2, 2009, but they later divorced. In July 2016, Keilar announced that she was engaged to Fernando Lujan, an active duty Green Beret who worked on the National Security Council at the White House. The couple got married on December 30, 2016, in Las Vegas, and have a son born on June 8, 2018. Keilar's experience as a military spouse has influenced her writing and reporting, particularly in her column Home Front. Overall, Keilar has built a distinguished career in journalism, covering a wide range of stories and earning numerous awards for her reporting.

title: Vanda Pignato
text:
Vanda Guiomar Pignato is a Brazilian-born Salvadoran lawyer, activist, politician, and former First Lady of El Salvador. Born on February 15, 1961, in São Paulo, Brazil, Pignato became the First Lady of El Salvador on June 1, 2009, when her husband, President Mauricio Funes, took office. At the same time, she was appointed as the country's Secretary of Social Inclusion, making her the first sitting First Lady in El Salvador's history to hold a political position.

Pignato's background is in activism, particularly in the Workers' Party, and she has worked closely with influential figures such as Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, former President of Brazil. She moved to El Salvador in 1992, where she represented the Workers' Party in Central America and later married Mauricio Funes. As First Lady and Secretary of Social Inclusion, Pignato has been a strong advocate for women's rights and gender equality. She has highlighted the challenges faced by Salvadoran women, including higher high school dropout rates and lower literacy rates than men, and economic dependence on male partners or family members.

One of Pignato's signature initiatives has been the establishment of Ciudad Mujer, a network of centers providing services to women, including healthcare, legal aid, financial advice, and career training. The centers, which were established in 2011, aim to provide a safe and supportive environment for women to access various services, including reproductive healthcare, neonatal care, and breast cancer prevention. By November 2014, an estimated 603,000 women had utilized Ciudad Mujer. The initiative has received international recognition, including from the Inter-American Development Bank and the United Nations.

Pignato's work has also had a broader impact, with other countries expressing interest in adopting similar initiatives. In 2015, the Brazilian government announced plans to launch its own "Women's House" project, modeled on Pignato's Ciudad Mujer program in El Salvador. Guatemala, Colombia, and Mexico have also expressed interest in implementing similar programs.

In addition to her work on women's issues, Pignato has been involved in responding to natural disasters, including severe flooding in 2011 that affected 70% of El Salvador. She traveled to Washington D.C. to lobby for humanitarian aid from the United States Congress and the U.S. State Department.

Pignato has received several awards and honors for her work, including the Ellis Island Medal of Honor in 2012. However, her personal life has also been subject to controversy, including her separation from her husband, Mauricio Funes, in 2014, and her diagnosis with cancer in 2015.

In 2018, a warrant was issued for Pignato's arrest as part of a case against her and her husband for alleged embezzlement and money laundering. The case involves allegations that Funes's first presidential campaign was financed by Brazilian company Odebrecht with illicit funds. Pignato's health condition was taken into consideration, but the judge decided that she posed a flight risk.

Throughout her career, Pignato has demonstrated a commitment to social justice and women's empowerment. Her initiatives, particularly Ciudad Mujer, have had a significant impact on the lives of women in El Salvador and beyond. Despite the challenges she has faced, Pignato remains a prominent figure in Salvadoran politics and a symbol of women's empowerment in the region.

title: Vadhir Derbez
text:
Vadhir Derbez is a Mexican actor, singer, and songwriter born on February 18, 1991, in Mexico City. He is the son of comic actor Eugenio Derbez, and his family background is deeply rooted in the entertainment industry. Vadhir's early life was marked by discipline and creativity, as he spent four years at the Culver Academies, a military school in the United States, where he developed his equestrian skills and even participated in Barack Obama's Inaugural parade in Washington D.C. in 2008.

Vadhir's acting career began at the tender age of six, when he appeared on the program "Derbez en Cuando" in 1997. He went on to participate in various television shows and soap operas, including "Cómplices Al Rescate," "La familia P. Luche," and "De pocas, pocas pulgas." His breakthrough role came in 2002 when he played a featured part in the novela "Cómplices Al Rescate." Throughout his career, Vadhir has worked with prominent production companies such as Televisa, Univision, Warner Brothers, Netflix, TV Azteca, and Telemundo.

In addition to his television work, Vadhir has also made a name for himself in the film industry. He made his film debut in 2005, providing the voice for the character Chuletas in the animated film "Imaginum." He then transitioned to live-action films, appearing in "Ladrones" in 2015 and "El tamaño si Importa" in 2016. One of his most notable roles was in the film "How to Be a Latin Lover" in 2017, where he played a younger version of his father's character.

Vadhir has also explored his musical side, making his music debut in 2016 with the release of his EP "Vadhir Derbez." The EP featured two singles: "Te Olvidé" and "Me Haces Sentir." He has since released several singles, including "Al Final," "Latin Lover," "Mala," and "Toda La Banda." His music career has been successful, with songs that showcase his versatility as an artist.

Throughout his career, Vadhir has demonstrated his versatility as an actor, singer, and songwriter. He has worked in various mediums, including television, film, and music, and has collaborated with prominent artists and production companies. His participation in reality TV shows, such as "Mira Quien Baila," where he won the first season, and "¿Quién es la máscara?," where he won the first season as Camaleon, have further solidified his reputation as a talented and dedicated artist.

In recent years, Vadhir has continued to work in film and television, appearing in projects such as "Sense8" and "Dulce familia." He has also expanded his musical horizons, releasing new singles and collaborating with other artists. With his talent, dedication, and passion for his craft, Vadhir Derbez is sure to continue making waves in the entertainment industry.

title: Cédric Bakambu
text:
Cédric Bakambu is a professional footballer who plays as a forward or winger for Real Betis and the DR Congo national team. Born on April 11, 1991, in Vitry-sur-Seine, Val-de-Marne, France, Bakambu began his career at local club Ivry at the age of 10 before transferring to Sochaux four years later. He made his professional debut for Sochaux in 2010 and played 107 official games for them over five seasons, scoring 21 goals.

Bakambu's performance at Sochaux caught the attention of Turkish club Bursaspor, who signed him in 2014 for €1.8 million. He had a successful season with Bursaspor, finishing as top scorer in the Turkish Cup and helping the team reach the final. In 2015, Bakambu joined Spanish side Villarreal, where he scored 9 goals in 34 games and was named in the UEFA Europa League Squad of the Season.

In 2018, Bakambu transferred to Beijing Guoan in the Chinese Super League, where he scored 22 goals in 45 games and won the Chinese FA Cup. He has also played for Marseille, Olympiacos, Al-Nasr, Galatasaray, and Real Betis. Bakambu has represented France at youth level, winning the 2010 UEFA European Under-19 Championship, but switched to represent DR Congo at senior level in 2015.

Bakambu has scored 12 goals in 43 appearances for DR Congo, helping the team qualify for the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations. He announced his retirement from international football in 2022 but later reversed his decision. Bakambu's versatility as a forward or winger, combined with his goal-scoring ability, make him a valuable asset to his team.

Throughout his career, Bakambu has received several individual honors, including the Turkish Cup Top Scorer, Facebook FA La Liga Best Breakthrough, Villarreal Rookie of the Year, and La Liga Player of the Month. He has also been named in the UEFA Europa League Squad of the Season and the Super League Greece Team of the Season.

Bakambu's personal life is marked by his cultural heritage, having grown up with both French and Congolese cultures. He and his international teammate Dieumerci Mbokani narrowly escaped a terrorist attack at Brussels Airport in 2016. With his successful career and personal achievements, Cédric Bakambu is a notable figure in the world of football.

title: Neil Googe
text:
Neil Googe is a British comics artist with a diverse body of work spanning various titles and publishers. His early career includes work on 2000 AD, a British comic book series, where he contributed to several Judge Dredd stories, as well as other titles such as Shotgun Mary and Mercy Heights. In 1999, Googe was hired to create a graphic novel adaptation of Konami's Silent Hill, but the project was ultimately cancelled due to disputes with Konami and its European branch, despite being completed and advertised.

In 2000, Googe co-founded the British independent comic publisher Com.x, where he created the series Bazooka Jules. Although only three issues were published, Googe has stated that he still has ideas for more stories. He has since worked on various projects in the American comic book market, including Welcome to Tranquility with writer Gail Simone for Wildstorm, where he also worked on Majestic. Other notable titles include Wildcats: World's End with Christos Gage and Dark Riders, a World of Warcraft hardback graphic novel with Mike Costa, published by DC Comics.

Googe has continued to work with DC Comics on one-shot issues, such as Rose and Thorn, Detective Comics Harley Quinn #1, and The Flash. He has also returned to 2000 AD to work on Survival Geeks, written by Gordon Rennie and Emma Beeby. Currently, Googe is working on a creator-owned project called Welcome to the Hood, which will be launched as a pen and paper Role Playing Game and accompanying comic. He is also revamping Bazooka Jules under the name Bazooka Jules: Tales from Caliber Bay, which will serve as a world setting for existing Role Playing Games systems with supplementary short stories in comic format.

In addition to his comic book work, Googe is also developing other tabletop and RPG products, including a 3rd party Pathfinder supplement. He has stated that he will continue to work on regular comic projects alongside his other endeavors. Throughout his career, Googe has worked with various writers, including Gail Simone, Christos Gage, and Mike Costa, and has contributed to a range of titles across different publishers.

title: Sada Thompson
text:
Sada Thompson was a renowned American actress who had a successful career in stage, film, and television. Born on September 27, 1927, in Des Moines, Iowa, she grew up in Fanwood, New Jersey, and attended Scotch Plains-Fanwood High School. Thompson developed an interest in theater at a young age and went on to earn a Bachelor of Fine Arts in Theatre from the Carnegie Institute of Technology, which is now known as Carnegie Mellon University.

Thompson began her career in regional theater, performing in various plays such as "The Seagull," "Pygmalion," and "Our Town." She received training at Pittsburgh Playhouse, where she appeared in numerous productions. She made her Off-Broadway debut in 1955 in a production of "Under Milk Wood" and later appeared on television in a 1956 production of "Goodyear Television Playhouse."

Thompson's Broadway debut came in 1959 with the musical "Juno," and she went on to appear in several other stage productions in New York City, including "The Effect of Gamma Rays on Man-in-the-Moon Marigolds," "Tartuffe," and "Twigs." Her performance in "Twigs" earned her a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play in 1972. Thompson's stage work also earned her an Obie Award, three Drama Desk Awards, and two Sarah Siddons Awards.

Thompson's television career took off in the 1970s, with her breakout role as Kate Lawrence in the TV series "Family," which she played from 1976 to 1980. Her portrayal of Kate earned her critical acclaim, and she won an Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series in 1978. She received a total of nine Emmy nominations throughout her career, including one for her guest role as Carla's mother on "Cheers."

In addition to her work on "Family," Thompson appeared in several other television shows, including "Owen Marshall: Counselor at Law," "The Love Boat," "Father Dowling Mysteries," and "ER." She also had roles in several films, including "The Pursuit of Happiness," "Desperate Characters," and "Pollock."

Thompson was married to Donald E. Stewart from 1949 until her death, and the couple had a daughter, Liza Stewart, who is a costume designer. Thompson passed away on May 4, 2011, at the age of 83, due to lung disease. Her legacy as a talented and versatile actress continues to be celebrated, and she remains one of the most respected figures in American theater and television.

title: Thirayuth Boonmee
text:
Thirayuth Boonmee is a Thai social scientist, public intellectual, and former student activist born on January 10, 1950. He rose to prominence as a student leader at Chulalongkorn University in 1973, where he played a key role in coordinating protests against the military dictatorship of Thanom Kittikachorn and Praphas Charusathien. As the leader of the National Student Center of Thailand (NSCT), Thirayuth helped organize tens of thousands of people in public demonstrations against the regime. One notable activity of the NSCT was a 10-day boycott of Japanese products, in protest against Japanese investments in Thailand.

In 1973, Thirayuth and 12 other student activists were arrested for sedition after distributing leaflets demanding a new constitution. The arrests sparked massive anti-government protests, with rumors spreading that the students had been killed. The demonstrations peaked on October 13, when around 400,000 protesters gathered in front of the Democracy Monument and the parliament building. Thirayuth and the other students were released that afternoon, and the king approved plans to draft a new constitution within 12 months.

Thirayuth also played a role in exposing the Internal Security Operations Command's role in a massacre of villagers at Ban Na Sai village in the northeast. After the student massacre at Thammasat University on October 6, 1976, Thirayuth fled to the jungle strongholds of the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT), where he became increasingly critical of the monarchy. In a broadcast on April 1, 1977, Thirayuth stated that the monarchy was "obsolete and deteriorating" and that its destruction would have no adverse effects.

In the early 1980s, Thirayuth returned to mainstream Thai intellectual life after the CPT dissolved itself. He later renounced socialism and rejected his anti-monarchical statements. Thirayuth pursued further education in the Netherlands, earning a doctorandus degree in Philosophy, Sociology, and Anthropology from the International Institute of Social Studies and the University of Nijmegen. He returned to Thailand in 1985 and began teaching at Thammasat University's Faculty of Sociology and Anthropology.

Thirayuth has held various positions at Thammasat University, including director of the Sanya Dharmasakti Institute for Democracy and Professor of Anthropology. In 1997, he was named one of Thailand's ten most influential public intellectuals. Thirayuth has been an outspoken critic of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, coining the term "Thaksinocracy" to describe his rule. Throughout his career, Thirayuth has been a prominent figure in Thai intellectual and social circles, known for his critiques of politics and society.

title: Michael L. MacDonald
text:
Michael L. MacDonald is a Canadian politician and Conservative member of the Canadian Senate, appointed on January 2, 2009, on the advice of Stephen Harper. Born on May 4, 1955, in Louisbourg, Nova Scotia, MacDonald is the youngest of 10 children. He graduated from the University of King's College in Halifax in 1977 with an Honours degree in political science.

MacDonald's entry into politics began in 1978 when he worked as a researcher for the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada Research Office. He then held various positions in the offices of several politicians, including MLA Gerald Sheehy, Premier John Buchanan, Thomas McMillan, and Stewart McInnes. In 1988, he became the owner of the Fortress Inn in Louisbourg, a business he still owns.

MacDonald has run for office several times, but has not been successful. In 1988, he ran federally in Cape Breton—East Richmond, placing second with 7,173 votes. He ran provincially in 1993 in the riding of Dartmouth-Cole Harbour, placing second with 2,905 votes, and again in 1998, placing third with 2,084 votes. In 2004, he ran federally in Dartmouth—Cole Harbour, placing third with 8,739 votes.

However, MacDonald has been involved in controversy. In February 2022, during the convoy protest in Ottawa, he was recorded making derisive remarks about the city's residents, expressing support for the protesters, and describing his wife as "a Karen" for wanting the protest to end. The video sparked outrage, and MacDonald later apologized in the Senate chamber.

In his personal life, MacDonald lives in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, with his wife Marilyn, and their two sons, Lauchlan and Liam. Despite the controversy, MacDonald remains a member of the Canadian Senate, appointed for life. His Senate appointment and subsequent career have been marked by both his dedication to public service and his involvement in controversy. 

Overall, MacDonald's life and career have been shaped by his education, family, and entry into politics. From his early days as a researcher to his current role as a Senator, MacDonald has navigated the complexities of Canadian politics, facing both successes and challenges along the way.

title: Yehuda Lindell
text:
Yehuda Lindell is an Israeli professor in the Department of Computer Science at Bar-Ilan University, where he conducts research on cryptography with a focus on the theory of secure computation and its application in practice. He was born on February 24, 1971, and received his BSc and MSc degrees in computer science from Bar-Ilan University. Lindell then obtained his PhD in computer science from the Weizmann Institute of Science in 2002.

After completing his PhD, Lindell received a Raviv Fellowship and spent two years at IBM's cryptography research group at the T.J. Watson Research Center. In 2004, he returned to Israel to take up an academic position at Bar-Ilan University. His work on secure computation was recognized by the award of an ERC starting grant in 2009 and an ERC consolidators grant in 2014. Lindell was appointed as an IACR Fellow in 2021.

In addition to his academic work, Lindell has industry experience, having worked as a permanent cryptographic consultant to Safenet from 2004 to 2014. He co-founded the company Unbound Security and served as its Chief Scientist from 2014 to 2018. In early 2019, he took over the role of CEO of Unbound Security, taking leave from Bar-Ilan University. In January 2022, Unbound Security was acquired by Coinbase, and Lindell now leads their cryptography team.

Lindell's main contributions are in the field of secure multiparty computation, with a focus on theoretical feasibility and practical applications. His research has focused on efficient two-party secure computation, multiparty computation for the multiparty honest-majority setting, and protocol composition. He has also worked on the design of two-party protocols that are secure against active adversaries and the introduction of covert adversarial models. Lindell's most cited work is a joint paper with Benny Pinkas on privacy-preserving data mining, which proposed the use of secure computation for performing data mining algorithms.

Lindell has received several awards for his work, including the IBM Pat Goldberg Memorial Best Paper Award in Computer Science, Electrical Engineering and Math in 2006 and the best paper award at ACM CCS 2016 for work on high-throughput MPC protocols. He is also the co-inventor of the AES-GCM-SIV mode of operation for symmetric encryption, which was standardized by the IETF Crypto Forum Research Group in RFC 8452.

In addition to his research and industry work, Lindell is also an author of several textbooks on cryptography, including "Introduction to Modern Cryptography" with Jonathan Katz, which is utilized in many universities around the world as a standard reference work. He has also edited several conference proceedings and published a review article on secure multiparty computation in the Communications of the ACM in 2021.

title: Jose Canseco
text:
José Canseco is a Cuban-American former professional baseball outfielder and designated hitter who played 17 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB). Born on July 2, 1964, in Havana, Cuba, Canseco grew up in a baseball-loving family and was the twin brother of Ozzie Canseco, who also played in the major leagues. The Canseco family moved to the Miami area in 1965, and José developed his baseball skills at Miami Coral Park High School.

The Oakland Athletics drafted Canseco in the 15th round of the 1982 Major League Baseball draft, and he made his professional debut in 1982 with the Miami Marlins of the Florida State League. Canseco quickly rose through the minor league ranks, earning the Baseball America Minor League Player of the Year Award in 1985. He made his major league debut with the Athletics on September 2, 1985, and played in 29 games that season, batting .302 with 5 home runs and 13 RBIs.

In 1986, Canseco won the American League Rookie of the Year award, hitting 33 home runs and 117 RBIs. He established himself as one of the premier power hitters in the game, and his impressive performance earned him a selection to the All-Star Game. Canseco followed up his rookie season with another strong performance in 1987, hitting 31 home runs and 113 RBIs.

The 1988 season was a standout year for Canseco, as he became the first player in MLB history to hit 40 home runs and steal 40 bases in one season. He hit 42 home runs, stole 40 bases, and drove in 124 runs, earning him the American League Most Valuable Player award. Canseco also won his first Silver Slugger Award and was named the American League's Player of the Month for September.

Canseco's success continued in the late 1980s and early 1990s, as he helped the Athletics win the World Series in 1989. He hit 17 home runs and 57 RBIs in 65 games that season, and his impressive performance earned him a selection to the All-Star Game. Canseco also won his second Silver Slugger Award in 1990.

Throughout his career, Canseco played for seven different teams, including the Athletics, New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox, Toronto Blue Jays, Texas Rangers, and St. Louis Cardinals. He averaged 40 home runs, 120 RBIs, and 102 runs scored every 162 games, and his 462 career home runs rank 12th-highest in American League history.

Despite his impressive statistics, Canseco's career was marked by injuries, particularly to his back. He underwent several surgeries and struggled with pain throughout his career. Canseco also faced controversy when he admitted to using performance-enhancing drugs during his playing career, which he detailed in his 2005 book, "Juiced: Wild Times, Rampant 'Roids, Smash Hits & How Baseball Got Big."

After retiring from baseball, Canseco pursued other interests, including boxing and mixed martial arts. He has remained in the public eye, and his legacy as one of the greatest power hitters of his generation continues to be celebrated by baseball fans around the world.

title: Jeffrey Satinover
text:
Jeffrey Satinover is an American psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and physicist born on September 4, 1947, in Chicago, Illinois. He earned multiple degrees from prestigious institutions, including a Bachelor of Science from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a Master of Education from Harvard University, a medical degree from the University of Texas, and a Master of Science in physics from Yale University. He also received a diploma in analytical psychology from the C. G. Jung Institute of Zürich, becoming their youngest graduate, and a PhD in physics from the University of Nice in France in 2009.

Satinover has written several books on various topics, including physics, neuroscience, and religion, but is perhaps best known for his work on homosexuality, same-sex marriage, and the ex-gay movement. His book, "Homosexuality and the Politics of Truth," published in 1996, debates the nature of homosexuality from psychological, religious, and scientific perspectives. In this book, Satinover argues that homosexuality is not a true illness but may be thought of as a "soul sickness" innate to human nature. He also suggests that gay activism distorts the truth and harms not only society but also homosexuals themselves.

Satinover has testified in several high-profile cases, including the 1997 trial in Florida challenging the state's law prohibiting adoption by gays and lesbians. He was called as an expert witness and surprisingly stated that he would have no objection to same-sex adoption if one of the adoptive parents was a man and the other a woman. However, he also stated that the needs of a child include having both a mother and a father.

In addition to his work on homosexuality, Satinover has also provided commentary for several documentary films, including "What the #$*! Do We (K)now!? " and "What the Bleep!?: Down the Rabbit Hole." He has also taught at various institutions, including King's College in New York City and the C. G. Jung Institute in Zürich. Satinover is a member of the scientific advisory committee of the National Association for Research & Therapy of Homosexuality and has written articles and testified on his views on same-sex marriage.

Satinover's eclectic worldview is reflected in his Jewish faith and his openness to exploring various spiritual and philosophical perspectives. He has written several books, including "The Empty Self: Gnostic & Jungian Foundations of Modern Identity" and "The Quantum Brain: The Search for Freedom and the Next Generation of Man." His work has been widely cited, and he has been a vocal advocate for his views on various topics.

Overall, Satinover's life and work reflect a complex and multifaceted individual who has made significant contributions to various fields, including psychiatry, physics, and public policy. His work on homosexuality and same-sex marriage has been particularly influential, and his views continue to be widely debated and discussed today.

title: Bobby Fischer
text:
Robert James Fischer was a chess prodigy who became the eleventh World Chess Champion. Born on March 9, 1943, in Chicago, Illinois, Fischer's mother, Regina Wender Fischer, was a US citizen born in Switzerland to Polish Jewish parents. Fischer's biological father may have been Paul Neményi, a Hungarian mathematician and physicist of Jewish heritage, rather than Hans-Gerhardt Fischer, a German biophysist.

Fischer learned to play chess at the age of six and quickly became engrossed in the game. His mother, Regina, sent a postcard to the Brooklyn Eagle newspaper seeking to place an ad to find other children to play chess with him. The ad was forwarded to Hermann Helms, the "Dean of American Chess," who introduced Fischer to Max Pavey, a former Scottish champion. Fischer played in a simultaneous exhibition against Pavey and, despite holding on for 15 minutes, eventually lost.

Fischer's chess career took off when he joined the Brooklyn Chess Club and began playing in tournaments. In 1956, he joined the Hawthorne Chess Club, where he played thousands of blitz and offhand games with strong players, studied chess books, and developed his skills. Fischer's first real tournament success came in July 1956, when he won the US Junior Chess Championship in Philadelphia at the age of 13.

Fischer's rise to fame continued as he played in top tournaments and against strong opponents. In 1957, he played a two-game match against former world champion Max Euwe, losing ½–1½. However, he soon earned the title of Master, becoming the youngest player to do so. Fischer won the US Championship in 1957/58, scoring 10½/13 and becoming the youngest-ever US Champion at the age of 14.

Fischer's success continued as he qualified for the 1958 Portorož Interzonal, where he earned a spot in the Candidates Tournament. He became the youngest person ever to qualify for the Candidates and the youngest-ever grandmaster at the time, aged 15 years, 6 months, and 1 day.

In the 1960s, Fischer continued to excel in chess, winning his first of a record eight US Championships at the age of 14. In 1964, he won the championship with an 11–0 score, the only perfect score in the history of the tournament. Fischer's success earned him a chance to challenge Boris Spassky for the World Chess Championship in 1972. The match, held in Reykjavík, Iceland, was a Cold War confrontation between the US and USSR that attracted worldwide attention.

Fischer won the championship match against Spassky, becoming the World Chess Champion. However, he refused to defend his title in 1975 when an agreement could not be reached with FIDE, the international governing body of chess. As a result, Anatoly Karpov was named World Champion by default.

Fischer disappeared from public life for many years but reemerged in 1992 to play an unofficial rematch against Spassky in Yugoslavia. His participation in the match led to a conflict with the US government, which had imposed sanctions on Yugoslavia.
