Fischer eventually lived as an émigré, and in 2004, he was arrested in Japan for using a revoked passport. He was granted Icelandic citizenship and lived there until his death in 2008.

Throughout his life, Fischer made significant contributions to chess, including writing the book "My 60 Memorable Games" and inventing Fischer random chess, also known as Chess960. However, he was also known for his antisemitic statements and Holocaust denial, which sparked controversy and speculation about his psychological condition. Fischer patented a modified chess timing system that added a time increment after each move, now a standard practice in top tournament and match play.

Fischer's life was marked by both brilliant chess achievements and personal turmoil. Despite his success, he struggled with fame and the pressures of being a chess prodigy. His legacy continues to be felt in the chess world, and his games remain a testament to his incredible skill and strategic thinking.

title: Kathleen A. McGrath
text:
Kathleen Anne McGrath was a trailblazing officer in the United States Navy, born on June 4, 1952, in Columbus, Ohio, to Colonel James H. McGrath and Martha McGrath. She grew up with a strong foundation and went on to earn a Bachelor of Science degree in Environmental Science from California State University, Sacramento, in 1975. McGrath furthered her education, earning a Master of Arts degree in Educational Management from Stanford University in 1987. She attended Officer Candidate School in Rhode Island, which marked the beginning of her distinguished naval career.

Before joining the US Navy in 1980, McGrath worked in the United States Forestry Service. Her naval career took her to various parts of the world, including the Western Pacific, the Persian Gulf, and the Mediterranean and Caribbean seas. In 1993 and 1994, McGrath commanded the rescue and salvage ship USS Recovery, making her one of the first women to command a US Navy ship. Although not a combatant ship, this was a significant milestone in her career.

In December 1998, McGrath took command of the frigate USS Jarrett, becoming the first woman to command a US Navy combatant ship. She was part of a group of five women, including Michelle J. Howard, Maureen Farren, Ann O'Connor, and Grace Mehl, chosen to be the first female combatant commanders in the United States Navy. McGrath's command of the USS Jarrett was a historic moment, coming just six years after Congress revoked rules prohibiting women from serving on combat aircraft and warships. In March 2000, McGrath commanded the USS Jarrett on a mission to the Persian Gulf region, where the ship hunted boats suspected of smuggling Iraqi oil in violation of United Nations sanctions.

Throughout her career, McGrath received numerous awards and decorations for her service, including the Legion of Merit, Meritorious Service Medal, Navy Commendation Medal, and Navy Achievement Medal, among others. She was promoted to the rank of captain in May 2002. After her tour as commander of the Jarrett, McGrath served at the Joint Advanced Warfighting Unit in Alexandria, Virginia.

McGrath's personal life was marked by her marriage to Gregory H. Brandon, with whom she had two children. Tragically, she died on September 26, 2002, at the age of 50, due to lung cancer at the National Naval Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. She was buried in Arlington National Cemetery, a testament to her dedication and service to her country. McGrath's legacy as a pioneering officer in the US Navy continues to inspire women in the military and beyond. Her achievements and awards serve as a reminder of her remarkable career and the impact she had on the US Navy.

title: Benjamin Lawrence Reid
text:
Benjamin Lawrence Reid was a distinguished American professor of English, born on May 3, 1918, in Louisville, Kentucky. His early life involved moving to Texas for a brief period, and during his childhood, he was an avid sportsman, playing baseball as a child and switching to basketball in his teens. Reid pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Arts from the University of Louisville in the 1940s. He furthered his education with a Master of Arts from Columbia University and a Doctor of Philosophy from the University of Virginia in the 1950s.

During World War II, Reid registered as a conscientious objector and served as a bridge constructor and a psychiatric hospital orderly. After the war, he began his academic career as an English lecturer at Iowa State College from 1946 to 1948. He then taught at Smith College from 1948 to 1951, before moving to Sweet Briar College, where he worked as an instructor from 1951 to 1957, and later as an assistant English professor.

In 1957, Reid joined Mount Holyoke College as an assistant professor, and over the years, he rose through the ranks, becoming associate professor in 1959, professor in 1963, and English professor in 1970. He spent the majority of his academic career at Mount Holyoke, teaching there until 1983. In addition to his academic pursuits, Reid was a prolific writer, publishing several books, including biographies of Gertrude Stein, William Butler Yeats, John Quinn, and Roger Casement. His notable works include "The Man from New York: John Quinn and His Friends," which earned him the Pulitzer Prize for Biography or Autobiography in 1969.

Reid's writing career spanned multiple genres, including biographies and autobiographies. His last publications were his autobiographies, which he wrote between 1988 and 1990. Throughout his career, Reid received several awards and honors for his work. In 1963, he received a research grant from the Fulbright Program to study at the University of London. He was also awarded a fellowship from the National Endowment for the Humanities in 1971 for his work on Russell. Furthermore, Reid was a finalist for the 1977 National Book Award for Biography and Autobiography for his book on Roger Casement.

Reid's contributions to literature and education were widely recognized. He was a dedicated academic, spending nearly four decades teaching and writing. His work continues to be celebrated for its insight into the lives of notable figures. Benjamin Lawrence Reid passed away on November 30, 1990, due to a heart attack and multiple strokes, in South Hadley, Massachusetts, leaving behind a legacy as a renowned professor and author. His work remains a testament to his dedication to literature and education.

title: Ahsee Tuala
text:
Ahsee Tuala is a Samoan rugby union player born on August 23, 1989, who currently plays as a fullback for Northampton Saints in the Aviva Premiership. He moved to New Zealand with his family at the age of two and grew up in South Auckland. Tuala began his senior rugby career in New Zealand with the Counties Manukau Steelers in 2009, at just 20 years old. His versatility in playing various positions across the backline made him an essential part of the Steelers squad, earning over 50 ITM Cup caps.

In 2015, Tuala signed with Northampton Saints in the Aviva Premiership, initially on a short-term deal until the end of the 2014-15 season. However, he impressed the team and signed a new deal, making his move permanent. During his time with Northampton Saints, Tuala had a breakthrough season in 2016-17, becoming a regular starter and scoring five tries. His performances earned him the Saints' Supporter' Breakthrough Player of the Year award.

Tuala has also had a significant impact in European rugby, helping Northampton Saints secure a spot in the European Rugby Champions Cup. He scored the match-winning try against Stade Francais, which clinched the final top-tier European spot. 

As for his international career, Tuala initially represented New Zealand in the under-20 and sevens teams. However, he later switched his allegiance to Samoa, making his international debut in 2014 against Canada. Tuala was named in the Samoan squad for the 2014 end-of-year rugby union tests and has since been called up to the team for the 2017 internationals, alongside his Northampton Saints teammate Ken Pisi. Throughout his career, Tuala has demonstrated his skills and adaptability as a player, and he continues to be an important part of both his club and international teams.

title: Jimmy Tompkins (priest)
text:
James John "Jimmy" Tompkins was a Roman Catholic priest who dedicated his life to improving the lives of people in northern and eastern Nova Scotia, Canada. Born on September 7, 1870, in Margaree Forks, Nova Scotia, Tompkins was deeply committed to education and believed in its power to bring about positive change. He attended St. Francis Xavier University, where he studied while also teaching Greek and mathematics to support himself. After completing his studies, Tompkins attended the Urban College in Rome, where he was ordained in 1902.

Tompkins returned to St. Francis Xavier University, where he taught and eventually became vice-rector. During his time at the university, he worked closely with the Carnegie Corporation to implement reform and modernization programs. One of his notable initiatives was an attempt to create a nondenominational university in the Maritime Provinces, which ultimately failed due to opposition from the Catholic Bishop of Antigonish. As a result, Tompkins was exiled to the fishing village of Canso, Nova Scotia, where he became the parish priest.

It was during his time in Canso that Tompkins observed firsthand the struggles of the poor fishing community and was inspired to take action. He helped organize and lead the Antigonish Movement, a progressive effort that incorporated adult education, cooperatives, and rural community development. The movement aimed to improve economic conditions and provide opportunities for people in the region. Tompkins believed that education was key to empowering people and often said, "It is not enough to have ideas, we have to put legs on them." He put this philosophy into practice by starting the first regional library in Nova Scotia, as well as the first credit union and a cooperative housing association in Reserve Mines, which was dubbed "Tompkinsville".

The Antigonish Movement eventually evolved into the Extension Department of St. Francis Xavier University, now known as the Coady International Center. Tompkins' work had a lasting impact on the community, and he is remembered as a champion of social justice and education. Throughout his career, Tompkins received several honors, including an honorary Doctor of Laws degree from Dalhousie University in 1919.

Tompkins continued to serve the community throughout his life, holding various positions, including parish priest and chaplain. He retired in 1948 due to ill health and lived at St. Martha's Convent in Margaree Forks, Nova Scotia. Tompkins passed away on May 5, 1953, at St. Martha's Hospital, and was buried in Reserve Mines. His legacy lives on through the Antigonish Movement and the Coady International Center, which continue to promote social justice and community development.

title: Vance Joy
text:
Vance Joy, born James Gabriel Keogh on December 1, 1987, is an Australian singer, songwriter, musician, and former Australian rules footballer. He is best known for his 2013 hit song "Riptide," which became a worldwide commercial success and helped launch his music career. Joy's early life was marked by a strong interest in music and sports. He attended St. Patrick's Primary School and later graduated from St Kevin's College, Toorak, in 2005. He also graduated from Monash University with a Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Laws.

Before pursuing a career in music, Joy was a promising Australian rules football player. He played for the Coburg Football Club in the Victorian Football League in 2008 and 2009, winning the best first year player award in 2008. However, he ultimately decided to pursue a career in music, citing that he "wasn't ever really in the mix (for the AFL)" and that his heart wasn't completely in football.

Joy's music career began in 2013 when he released his debut single "From Afar" and his debut EP "God Loves You When You're Dancing" in March 2013. The EP included the hit single "Riptide," which peaked at number 6 on the ARIA Singles Chart and was certified nine times platinum by the Australian Record Industry Association (ARIA). The song's success led to Joy signing a five-album deal with Atlantic Records and releasing his debut studio album "Dream Your Life Away" in 2014. The album was a commercial success, and Joy won the Best Male Artist category at the ARIA Music Awards of 2015.

Joy's subsequent albums, "Nation of Two" (2018) and "In Our Own Sweet Time" (2022), also received critical acclaim and commercial success. He has collaborated with other artists, including Benny Blanco and Marshmello, and has toured extensively, including as an opening act for Taylor Swift's 1989 World Tour and P!nk's Beautiful Trauma World Tour. Joy has also been recognized for his songwriting skills, winning the International Songwriting Competition (ISC) for "Riptide" in 2015.

In his personal life, Joy announced his engagement to Selen Us in November 2022, and they married in June 2023. The couple welcomed their daughter Gigi in early 2024. Joy's music often reflects his personal experiences, including his song "Missing Piece," which was inspired by his wife.

Throughout his career, Joy has been nominated for numerous awards and has won several, including the ARIA Award for Best Male Artist and the International Songwriting Competition. He continues to tour and release new music, with his most recent album "In Our Own Sweet Time" debuting in 2022. With his soulful voice and introspective songwriting, Vance Joy has established himself as a prominent figure in the music industry.

title: Djimon Hounsou
text:
Djimon Hounsou is a Beninese-American actor born on April 24, 1964, in Cotonou, Benin, to Albertine and Pierre Hounsou. At the age of 12, he immigrated to Lyon, France, with his brother Edmond, where he eventually dropped out of school and experienced homelessness. However, a chance meeting with a photographer led to an introduction to fashion designer Thierry Mugler, who encouraged Hounsou to pursue a modeling career. In 1987, he began his modeling career in Paris and later moved to the United States in 1990.

Hounsou's early career involved appearing in music videos, including "Straight Up" by Paula Abdul, "I Don't Wanna Lose You" by Tina Turner, and Madonna's "Express Yourself." He made his film debut in 1990 in the Sandra Bernhard film Without You I'm Nothing. He went on to appear in television shows such as Beverly Hills, 90210 and ER, and had a guest starring role on Alias. One of his early notable roles was in the science fiction film Stargate.

Hounsou's breakthrough role came in 1997 when he played Cinqué in Steven Spielberg's film Amistad, earning him a Golden Globe nomination. He continued to gain recognition with roles in films such as Gladiator (2000), In America (2002), and Blood Diamond (2006), for which he received Academy Award nominations for Best Supporting Actor. His performances in these films solidified his position as a talented and versatile actor.

In addition to his film work, Hounsou has also ventured into directing. He made his directorial debut with the documentary film In Search of Voodoo: Roots to Heaven (2018), which explores the history and practices of West African Vodun. Hounsou has also been involved in various other projects, including narrating ESPN's "32 Teams, 1 Dream" commercials for the 2010 FIFA World Cup and speaking at the Summit on Climate Change at the United Nations.

Hounsou has also appeared in several Marvel and DC films, including Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), Captain Marvel (2019), Aquaman (2018), Shazam! (2019), Black Adam (2022), and Shazam! Fury of the Gods (2023). He has also voiced characters in animated films and series, such as How to Train Your Dragon 2 and What If...?.

In his personal life, Hounsou has been in a relationship with model Kimora Lee Simmons, with whom he has a son. The couple had a traditional commitment ceremony in 2008, but did not legally marry in the United States. They announced their separation in 2012. Throughout his career, Hounsou has faced challenges as a Black actor in Hollywood, including typecasting and unfair compensation. Despite his success and multiple award nominations, he has spoken publicly about the financial struggles he has faced and the systemic racism he believes is responsible for these challenges.

In recent years, Hounsou has continued to appear in a wide range of films, including Furious 7 (2015), The Legend of Tarzan (2016), A Quiet Place Part II (2021), and Gran Turismo (2023). With a career spanning over three decades, Djimon Hounsou has established himself as a talented and versatile actor, director, and advocate for social and environmental causes. His dedication to his craft and his commitment to using his platform to raise awareness about important issues have made him a respected figure in the entertainment industry.

title: Elizabeth Inglis
text:
Elizabeth Inglis was a British actress born Desiree Mary Lucy Hawkins on July 10, 1913, in Colchester, England, to Margaret Inglis and Alan George Hawkins. She began her acting career in the 1930s, making her screen debut in the 1934 film "Borrowed Clothes." One of her early notable roles was a small part as Hilary Jordan in Alfred Hitchcock's 1935 film "The 39 Steps." 

Inglis also had a significant stage career, playing the role of Nancy, the young maid, in the original British production of Patrick Hamilton's play "Gas Light" in 1938-1939. The production ran for 141 performances, and Inglis and the rest of the cast recreated their stage roles for a live television presentation on BBC Television in 1939.

In Hollywood, Inglis played the role of Adele Ainsworth in William Wyler's film "The Letter" in 1940, by which time she was using the stage name Elizabeth Earl. After marrying American television executive Pat Weaver in 1942, Inglis retired from acting to focus on her family. The couple had two children, including actress Sigourney Weaver, who would go on to become a renowned actress in her own right.

Inglis's connection to her daughter's iconic film franchise was evident in a deleted scene from the 1986 film "Aliens," in which a photograph of Inglis was used to portray Amanda Ripley, the elderly daughter of Sigourney Weaver's character Ellen Ripley. 

Elizabeth Inglis passed away on August 25, 2007, at the age of 94, in Santa Barbara, California, leaving behind a legacy as a pioneering actress and the mother of one of Hollywood's most beloved stars.

title: Susan Sarandon
text:
Susan Sarandon is a renowned American actress with a career spanning over five decades. Born on October 4, 1946, in Jackson Heights, Queens, New York City, she is the eldest of nine children to Lenora Marie and Phillip Leslie Tomalin. Her early life was marked by a move to New Jersey, where she was raised in a Roman Catholic family and attended Saint Francis Grammar School and Edison High School.

Sarandon's interest in acting began at a young age, and she attended the Catholic University of America in Washington D.C., where she earned a Bachelor of Arts in drama. After college, she supported herself by working various jobs, including emptying bedpans in a hospital, cutting hair, and cleaning houses. In 1968, she and her then-husband Chris appeared on stage at the Wayside Theatre in Middletown, Virginia, which marked the beginning of her career in the entertainment industry.

Sarandon made her film debut in Joe (1970) and went on to appear in several soap operas, including A World Apart and Search for Tomorrow. Her breakthrough role came in 1975 with the cult favorite The Rocky Horror Picture Show. She gained critical acclaim for her performances in films such as Pretty Baby (1978), The Hunger (1983), and Bull Durham (1988). Her portrayal of Louise Sawyer in Thelma & Louise (1991) and Michaela Odone in Lorenzo's Oil (1992) earned her Academy Award nominations.

In 1995, Sarandon won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her role as Sister Helen Prejean in Dead Man Walking. This role cemented her status as a leading lady in Hollywood, and she went on to appear in a wide range of films, including Little Women (1994), Stepmom (1998), and Enchanted (2007). Her performances have been recognized with numerous awards and nominations, including a British Academy Film Award and several Golden Globe nominations.

In addition to her acting career, Sarandon is known for her social and political activism. She has been a vocal advocate for progressive causes, including anti-war efforts, women's rights, and LGBTQ+ rights. In 1999, she was appointed a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador and has since worked with various organizations to promote social justice and human rights. She has also been involved in several high-profile campaigns, including the campaign to free Richard Glossip, a man on death row in Oklahoma.

Sarandon has also been involved in various charitable endeavors, including supporting organizations that provide aid to refugees and advocating for the rights of marginalized communities. In 2010, she was appointed an FAO Goodwill Ambassador, and in 2018, she donated fruit trees to the New York City Housing Authority's Jamaica Houses.

Throughout her career, Sarandon has been recognized for her contributions to the entertainment industry and social activism. She has received several awards, including the Action Against Hunger Humanitarian Award and the Women in Film Crystal Award. Her legacy as a talented actress and dedicated activist continues to inspire new generations of artists and social justice advocates.

Sarandon's personal life has been subject to media attention, including her high-profile relationships and her support for various presidential candidates. In 2016, she endorsed Green Party candidate Jill Stein for president, and in 2017, she portrayed Bette Davis in the FX miniseries Feud. Her commitment to social justice and human rights continues to be an integral part of her career and public persona.

In recent years, Sarandon has continued to act in film and television, appearing in projects such as The Meddler (2015), A Bad Moms Christmas (2017), and the FOX TV drama Monarch (2022). Her dedication to social activism and her passion for promoting human rights and social justice have made her one of the most respected and beloved figures in the entertainment industry. With a career spanning over five decades, Sarandon has established herself as a talented actress and a dedicated advocate for social justice and human rights.

title: Don DeLillo
text:
Donald DeLillo is a renowned American novelist, short story writer, playwright, screenwriter, and essayist, born on November 20, 1936, in New York City. His works cover a wide range of subjects, including consumerism, nuclear war, language, art, television, the Digital Age, mathematics, politics, economics, and sports. DeLillo's writing often explores the themes of living in "dangerous times" and the "inner life of the culture."

Growing up in an Italian-American neighborhood in the Bronx, DeLillo was the eldest of eleven children in a Catholic family. His childhood experiences, including pretending to be a baseball announcer on the radio, fostered his creative imagination. As a teenager, DeLillo developed a love for reading, which became a lifelong habit. He was influenced by modernist fiction, jazz music, and postwar cinema, citing artists such as Ornette Coleman, Miles Davis, and filmmakers like Antonioni and Godard.

DeLillo's early life and education also played a significant role in shaping his writing style. He graduated from Cardinal Hayes High School in 1954 and Fordham University in 1958 with a degree in communication arts. After college, he worked as a copywriter at Ogilvy & Mather, writing image ads for Sears Roebuck, among others. However, DeLillo quit his job in 1964 to pursue a career in writing.

DeLillo's first short story, "The River Jordan," was published in 1960, and he began working on his first novel, Americana, in 1966. The novel was finally published in 1971 to modest critical praise. Over the next several years, DeLillo published several novels, including End Zone (1972), Great Jones Street (1973), Ratner's Star (1976), Players (1977), and Running Dog (1978). These works showcased DeLillo's unique writing style, which often explored the complexities of American culture and society.

In the 1980s, DeLillo's writing career gained momentum with the publication of The Names (1982) and White Noise (1985). The latter novel brought DeLillo widespread recognition and the National Book Award for Fiction. White Noise was a major breakthrough for DeLillo, earning him a place in the canon of contemporary postmodern novelists. The novel's influence can be seen in the writing of several authors, including David Foster Wallace and Jonathan Lethem.

DeLillo's subsequent novels, including Libra (1988) and Underworld (1997), solidified his reputation as a major literary figure. Libra, a speculative fictionalized life of Lee Harvey Oswald, became an international bestseller and won several awards. Underworld, a historical novel that explores American history from the 1940s to the 1980s, earned DeLillo the PEN/Faulkner Award and the William Dean Howells Medal.

Throughout his career, DeLillo has been recognized for his contributions to literature. He has received several awards, including the Jerusalem Prize, the PEN/Saul Bellow Award for Achievement in American Fiction, and the Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction. DeLillo's works continue to be widely read and studied today, offering insightful commentary on American culture and society.

DeLillo's writing often explores the tensions between individual experience and broader cultural and historical contexts. His novels frequently incorporate elements of popular culture, history, and politics, blurring the lines between fact and fiction. Through his writing, DeLillo seeks to challenge readers' assumptions about the world around them, encouraging them to think critically about the complexities of modern life.

In his own words, DeLillo believes that writers "must oppose systems" and challenge the power structures that shape our lives. His writing continues to be characterized by its unique blend of literary innovation, philosophical depth, and cultural commentary, making him one of the most important American writers of his generation.

title: Michael Collins (astronaut)
text:
Michael Collins was an American astronaut born on October 31, 1930, in Rome, Italy, to a military family. His father, James Lawton Collins, was a U.S. Army officer serving as the military attaché in Rome at the time of Michael's birth. Collins spent his childhood moving between various locations, including Oklahoma, New York, Maryland, Ohio, Puerto Rico, Texas, and Virginia, due to his father's military postings. He attended several schools, including the Academia del Perpetuo Socorro in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and St. Albans School in Washington, D.C.

Collins decided to follow in his family's tradition of military service and was appointed to the United States Military Academy at West Point, New York. He graduated in 1952 with a Bachelor of Science degree in military science. Collins then joined the United States Air Force and began his training as a fighter pilot. He flew F-86 Sabre jets in France and later became a test pilot at the USAF Experimental Flight Test Pilot School at Edwards Air Force Base in California.

In 1963, Collins was selected as part of NASA's third group of astronauts. He flew in space twice, first on Gemini 10 in 1966, where he and command pilot John Young performed orbital rendezvous with two spacecraft and undertook two extravehicular activities. Collins became the fourth person to perform a spacewalk and the first person to have performed more than one spacewalk.

Collins' most notable mission was as the command module pilot for Apollo 11 in 1969. He orbited the Moon in the command module Columbia while his crewmates, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, made the first crewed landing on the Moon's surface. Collins became one of 24 people to fly to the Moon and orbited it thirty times.

After retiring from NASA in 1970, Collins pursued a career in politics and public service. He worked in the Department of State as Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs and later became the director of the National Air and Space Museum. Collins also served as undersecretary of the Smithsonian Institution and worked as a consultant.

Throughout his career, Collins received numerous awards and honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and the Congressional Gold Medal. He was married to Patricia Mary Finnegan and had three children, including actress Kate Collins. Collins passed away on April 28, 2021, at the age of 90.

Collins' contributions to the space program were significant, and his experiences as an astronaut and test pilot provided valuable insights into the development of space exploration. His participation in the Apollo 11 mission and his role in the Gemini program demonstrate his dedication to the advancement of space travel and exploration.

The details of Collins' early life, education, and military service provide a comprehensive understanding of his background and motivations. His selection as an astronaut and his subsequent missions demonstrate his exceptional abilities and qualifications. Collins' legacy as an astronaut and his contributions to the space program continue to inspire future generations of space explorers.

In conclusion, Michael Collins was a remarkable individual who made significant contributions to the space program. His experiences as an astronaut, test pilot, and public servant demonstrate his dedication to the advancement of space exploration and his commitment to public service. Collins' legacy continues to inspire and motivate people around the world.

title: Fifi Cooper
text:
Refilwe Boingotlo Moeketsi, known professionally as Fifi Cooper, is a South African recording artist born on October 24, 1991. She began her music career as an R&B singer at a young age and later explored rap, showcasing her musical versatility. Fifi Cooper's early education took place in Montshiwa, Mahikeng, South Africa, where she developed her singing and dancing skills. She completed her secondary education at Batswana High School, Mahikeng, and went on to study Media at Boston Media House.

Fifi Cooper started singing at the age of 8 and professionally began her music career in 2008 with a guest appearance on Mo'Molemi's album, Motzamai: Rebel With a Pause. Her breakthrough came in 2010 with the release of her rap single "Chechela Morago," which gained massive airplay and helped her gain recognition in the South African music industry. She also made vocal appearances on several albums, including AKA's "Baddest Remix" single and Khuli Chana's Lost in Time.

In 2015, Fifi Cooper signed with Ambitiouz Entertainment and released her debut studio album, 20FIFI, which won three awards at the 15th Metro FM Music Awards. The album was also nominated for "Best Newcomer of The Year" and "Best Female Artist of The Year" at the 2nd edition of the South African Music Awards. The album's success was marked by the release of singles such as "Kisses," which had a music video directed by Dino Benedetti.

However, Fifi Cooper's career was affected by her departure from Ambitiouz Entertainment in 2017, along with A-Reece and B3nchMarQ. A court case ensued, and the label successfully sued her for copyright infringement. The court ruling meant that Fifi Cooper no longer had ownership of her songs recorded under the label and was required to pay damages and cover legal costs. Fortunately, the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) intervened, and with their support, Fifi Cooper negotiated an out-of-court settlement that restored her rights to perform her music.

After the dispute, Fifi Cooper founded her own record label, Mo Cooper Records, and released her album "Take Me Back" with 21 tracks featuring various artists. In 2020, she released her single "Net So" off her upcoming album titled Chapters. The music video for "Net So" was written and directed by Fifi Cooper herself. She released another single, "Motlogeleng," in March 2021.

Fifi Cooper is regarded as the "Motswako first lady" and is known for her musical versatility, rapping and singing in hip hop and Motswako genres. Her style of rap is described as unpredictable, punchy, and hearty. As a single mother, Fifi Cooper has a son named Resego and continues to make music, having released several albums and singles throughout her career.

title: Maddy Crippen
text:
Madeleine Marie Crippen, also known as Maddy Crippen or Madeleine Plankey, is a former American competition swimmer born on July 10, 1980. She represented the United States at the 2000 Summer Olympics, where she placed sixth in the 400-meter individual medley event. Crippen's swimming career was marked by several notable achievements, including a silver medal at the 1997 Pan Pacific Championship in Fukuoka, Japan, as part of Team USA. She also placed fifth in the 400-meter individual medley and sixth in the 200-meter individual medley at the 1998 World Aquatics Championships in Perth, Australia.

In 1999, Crippen represented the United States at the Pan Pacific Championships, where she placed fourth in the 400-meter individual medley. She earned a spot on the 2000 Olympic Team by placing second in the 400-meter individual medley at the U.S. Olympic Trials. Crippen's Olympic coaches included Hall of Fame Coach Dick Shoulberg, who served as an Advisory Women's Coach.

Crippen is a three-time U.S. national champion, winning two national titles in the 400-meter individual medley and one in the 200-meter breaststroke. During her college swimming career at Villanova University, she swam for the Villanova Wildcats and won an NCAA championship in the 400-yard individual medley. Crippen also won ten Big East championships and was named Big East "Swimmer of the Year" in 1999 and 2001. She was inducted into the Villanova Athletic Hall of Fame in 2019.

Crippen comes from a swimming family. Her brother, Fran, was a bronze medalist in the 10-kilometer open water race at the 2009 World Aquatics Championships and swam for the University of Virginia. He tragically passed away in 2010. Her sisters, Claire and Teresa, are also accomplished swimmers. Claire is a national finalist and NCAA All-American, while Teresa is a Pan American Games Champion and U.S. National Team member.

After retiring from swimming in 2004, Crippen worked as a marketing professional. She was also involved in USA Swimming, serving on the board of directors and the Athletes Executive Committee. Crippen is married to Sean Plankey, a commander in the U.S. Coast Guard.

title: Ramli Sarip
text:
Ramli Sarip, also known as "Papa Rock", is a Singaporean musician, singer, songwriter, arranger, and record producer who has been a pioneer of the country's rock scene. Born on October 15, 1952, Ramli has had a long and illustrious career spanning over five decades. He was the frontman and lead singer of the Singapore-based heavy metal-rock group Sweet Charity, which was established in 1964 and achieved immense success in the 1970s and 1980s, igniting a "rock explosion" in both Singapore and Malaysia. Ramli left Sweet Charity in 1986 and pursued a solo career, becoming the first Malay rock singer to hold two solo concerts at the Istana Budaya in Kuala Lumpur.

During his solo career, Ramli was signed under Warner Music and released 12 solo albums as of 2011. He also formed a five-piece band called Sangkakala to serve as his backing band. In 1990, he hosted a Malaysian Hari Raya Puasa television special called Bersama Ramli Sarip, which was released on the first day of the season. However, Radio Televisyen Malaysia imposed a seven-year ban on him in 1993 due to his long hair, which was against the broadcaster's rules at the time.

Ramli has received several awards and honors for his contributions to music. In 1998, he was awarded the COMPASS Artistic Excellence Award. In 2013, he was conferred the title of 'Datuk' by the Yang di-Pertua Negeri of the State of Malacca, a rare honor that recognizes his contributions to the music industry. He was also awarded the Companion Class II of the Exalted Order of Malacca (DPSM) for his services.

In addition to his music career, Ramli has also ventured into acting, starring in the Singaporean satirical film Talking Cock the Movie in 2002. In 2011, he was a vocalist for the remake of "Home". Ramli has also been involved in some controversy, particularly in 2019 when he performed a rendition of Singapore's national anthem, "Majulah Singapura", which received criticism from some quarters, including Dr. Rohana Zubir, the daughter of the original composer Zubir Said. Despite this, Ramli performed the national anthem again at the 2019 National Day Parade.

Throughout his career, Ramli has been known for his contributions to Singapore's music scene, and his legacy continues to be celebrated by fans and fellow musicians alike. His dedication to his craft has earned him the respect of his peers, and his influence can still be seen in the music industry today. With a career spanning over 50 years, Ramli Sarip remains a beloved figure in Singaporean music, and his impact on the country's rock scene will not be forgotten. Ramli's ability to adapt to changing musical trends and his willingness to experiment with different genres have kept him relevant in the ever-evolving music industry. His iconic status as "Papa Rock" continues to inspire new generations of musicians and fans alike.

title: Lali Espósito
text:
Lali Espósito, born Mariana "Lali" Espósito on October 10, 1991, in Buenos Aires, Argentina, is a multifaceted artist who has made a significant impact in the entertainment industry. She began her career at the age of six on the children's program Caramelito y Vos and later landed a role in the children's telenovela Rincón de Luz in 2003. Her early start in television led to roles in other telenovelas, including Floricienta and Chiquititas, which helped establish her as a child actress.

Espósito's breakthrough role came in 2007 when she played Marianella "Mar" Rinaldi in the telenovela Casi Ángeles, which became a huge success in Argentina, Latin America, and Israel. The show ran for three seasons and earned her a household name. During this time, she also became a member of the pop band Teen Angels, which was formed from the television series. The group released six studio albums, with five of them being certified platinum and one certified gold in Argentina.

After Casi Ángeles ended in 2010, Espósito adopted the stage name Lali and pursued a solo music career. She released her debut solo studio album, A Bailar, in 2014, which was a commercial success and spawned hit singles like "Asesina," "Mil Años Luz," and "Histeria." The album was certified gold in Argentina, and the A Bailar Tour, which followed, was a huge success, earning millions and becoming the highest-grossing tour of 2015 in Argentina.

Espósito continued to release successful albums, including Soy in 2016, Brava in 2018, and Libra in 2020. Her music has been influenced by pop and EDM, and she has collaborated with artists like Abraham Mateo, Brian Cross, and Baby K. Her tours, including the Soy Tour and Brava Tour, have also been well-received.

In addition to her music career, Espósito has also made a name for herself in acting, starring in telenovelas, films, and television comedies. Her notable roles include Abigail Williams in the Buenos Aires production of The Crucible and her performances in the crime-thriller film The Accused and Netflix's action crime drama television series Sky Rojo. She has received critical acclaim for her portrayals and has been nominated for several awards, including the Lo Nuestro Awards and the Seoul International Drama Awards.

Throughout her career, Espósito has received numerous awards and nominations, including six Gardel Awards, five MTV Europe Music Awards, thirteen Argentina Kids' Choice Awards, one Billboard Latin Music Award, and seven MTV Millennial Awards. In 2015, she was named one of the ten most influential women in Argentina by Infobae, a testament to her impact and influence in the entertainment industry.

With her versatility and talent, Espósito has become a household name in Latin America, the Middle East, and Europe. Her dedication to her craft and her ability to connect with her audience have made her one of the most successful and influential artists in the industry today.

title: Francis Nicholson (painter)
text:
Francis Nicholson was a British artist born on November 14, 1753, in Pickering, North Yorkshire. He was a versatile artist who worked in both watercolour and oil, but is primarily known for his landscape paintings. Nicholson's early life and training are not well-documented, but it is known that he studied with a local artist in Scarborough before starting his career in his hometown of Pickering. Initially, he produced sporting pictures and portraits for patrons in Yorkshire, but soon shifted his focus to landscapes and topographical paintings.

In the mid-1780s, Nicholson began creating paintings of country houses, which led him to concentrate on landscapes in watercolour. His work gained recognition, and from 1789, he contributed views of Yorkshire and Scotland to exhibitions at the Royal Academy. He also provided topographical views for the Copper Plate Magazine and collaborated with engraver Francis Jukes on "The Beauties of England and Wales", a multi-volume publication that showcased his skills as a landscape artist.

Although Nicholson's market became increasingly based in London, he continued to live in Yorkshire, residing in Whitby, Knaresborough, and Ripon. It wasn't until around 1803 that he finally moved to London. In 1804, he became a founder-member of the Society of Painters in Watercolours, a organization that aimed to promote and exhibit watercolour art. Nicholson was a prolific contributor to the society's exhibitions and remained a prominent figure in the art world.

In addition to his artistic pursuits, Nicholson wrote a handbook titled "The practice of drawing and painting landscape from nature, in water colours", which was published in 1820. The book was a success, and a second edition was published in 1823. Nicholson passed away on March 6, 1844, in London, where he is buried in Brompton Cemetery.

Nicholson's legacy is significant, and he is often referred to as the "Father of water colour painting". He was also an early pioneer of lithography and was admired by the renowned artist J.M.W. Turner. A self-portrait of Nicholson, created around 1837, is now part of the National Portrait Gallery's collection. In 2012, a Blue Plaque was erected in his memory in Pickering, his hometown. Nicholson's daughter, Marianne Croker, was also an artist, poet, and author, and married Thomas Crofton Croker, further solidifying her father's artistic legacy.

title: Josiah Maduabuchi
text:
Josiah Maduabuchi is a Nigerian footballer born on April 16, 1988, in Lagos. He plays as a midfielder and has had a career spanning several clubs. Maduabuchi began his football career with Wikki Tourists F.C. before moving to Enyimba International in 2007, where he likely gained more experience and exposure. After spending several years with Enyimba International, he joined Lobi Stars in 2015, marking a new chapter in his club career.

In addition to his club career, Maduabuchi has also been recognized at the international level. On April 15, 2010, he received his first call-up to the Nigeria national team, which was a significant milestone in his career. He was part of the training camp for the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, indicating that he was considered a valuable player for the team.

Maduabuchi is known for his versatility as a central attacking midfielder, which allows him to play in various positions and adapt to different playing styles. His ability to play in multiple positions makes him a valuable asset to his team, as he can be deployed in different roles to suit the team's needs.

Throughout his career, Maduabuchi has demonstrated his potential as a skilled footballer, and his call-up to the national team was a testament to his abilities. With his experience and versatility, he has likely made significant contributions to his teams, both at the club and international levels. Currently, Maduabuchi plays for Lobi Stars, where he continues to showcase his skills as a midfielder.

title: Will Voigt
text:
William Voigt is an American basketball coach with a diverse coaching background spanning various levels, including professional, minor league, and collegiate basketball in the United States and internationally. Born on August 18, 1976, Voigt grew up in Cabot, Vermont, and attended Cabot High School, where he played varsity basketball and soccer. He later attended Pomona College in California, where he lettered in soccer and graduated with a degree in political science.

Voigt's coaching career began with an internship with the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers while he was still in college. After graduation, he became a video coordinator with the San Antonio Spurs and later entered the college coaching ranks as an assistant with the University of Texas under Rick Barnes. He then moved to Metro State as an assistant coach under Mike Dunlap.

Voigt's first head coaching position was with Ulriken Elite in Norway from 2003 to 2006. He then returned to his home state of Vermont to coach the Vermont Frost Heaves, leading the team to back-to-back ABA Championships. In 2009, he was selected by fans to be the head coach of the Bakersfield Jam of the NBA Development League, where he led the team to three playoff appearances.

In the following years, Voigt coached in various international leagues, including the Chinese Basketball Association and the Nigerian national team, which he led to its first AfroBasket title and automatic qualification to the 2016 Summer Olympics. He also coached the Angola national team and the German Bundesliga side Telekom Baskets Bonn.

In 2022, Voigt signed a one-year deal as head coach of Zamalek of the Egyptian Basketball Super League and the Basketball Africa League (BAL), guiding the team to the third place in the 2022 BAL Playoffs and the semi-finals of the Super League. He then became the head coach of the Austin Spurs of the NBA G League in June 2023.

Most recently, on June 3, 2024, Brigham Young University announced that Voigt would join their men's basketball team as an assistant coach. Throughout his coaching career, Voigt has demonstrated his versatility and ability to adapt to different teams and leagues. He is the son of former Vermont Poet Laureate Ellen Bryant Voigt.

title: Loo Kum Zee
text:
Loo Kum Zee is a Malaysian high jumper born on December 2, 1974. He has achieved a personal best jump of 2.24 metres, which he accomplished in Chiangmai in December 1995. Throughout his career, Loo has won several bronze medals at the Asian Championships, specifically in the years 1995, 1998, 2002, and 2003. He has also had the opportunity to compete at the Olympic Games, representing Malaysia in the 1996 event, although he did not make it to the final.

In his early life, Loo attended secondary school at SMJK Sam Tet in Ipoh, Perak. His achievements in sports have been recognized by the Malaysian government, as he was awarded the Member of the Order of the Defender of the Realm (A.M.N.) in 2013. This honour is a testament to his contributions to the country's sports scene.

As a high jumper, Loo has demonstrated his skills and dedication to his craft, achieving notable results in various competitions. His personal best jump of 2.24 metres remains a remarkable achievement, and his bronze medals at the Asian Championships showcase his consistency and talent. His participation in the 1996 Olympic Games was also a significant experience, allowing him to compete on a global stage.

Overall, Loo Kum Zee is a respected figure in Malaysian athletics, with a career marked by notable achievements and recognition from the government. His accomplishments serve as an inspiration to aspiring athletes, and his legacy continues to be celebrated in the sports community.

title: Thomas Jack
text:
Thomas Jack, born Tom Jack Johnston, is an Australian DJ, record producer, and musician who has made a significant impact on the music scene with his unique style of tropical house music. Growing up on a dairy farm in a small rural town in New South Wales, Johnston's early life was far removed from the glamour of the music industry. However, his interest in music production began when he was a teenager, using the PlayStation game eJay to produce dance music. He later moved to Ableton, a software that would become instrumental in shaping his sound.

Johnston's entry into the music industry was marked by his move to Sydney to enroll in a music production school. It was during this time that he developed his skills and began to make a name for himself in the music scene. He started using various stage names, including Dirty-D, Bassics, Tommy, and Tom Foolery, but it wasn't until he adopted the stage name Thomas Jack that he began to gain recognition.

Thomas Jack's music style is characterized by its summery, laid-back, and uplifting feel, often featuring live instruments such as saxophone, flute, piano, and guitar. His tracks often include samples of speeches, adding a unique element to his sound. Jack's music is inspired by deep house, acoustic rock, and jam bands, and he has cited his desire to create a distinct sound that blends different styles.

In 2013, Jack began a podcast mix series called Tropical House, which featured guest mixes by prominent artists in the genre. His original tracks, such as "Symphony" and "The Final Speech," as well as his remixes of popular artists like Of Monsters & Men and OneRepublic, gained him recognition across EDM websites. Jack's busy touring schedule took him to clubs around the globe, and he has spent a considerable amount of time in the United States, particularly in Florida.

One of Jack's most notable achievements is his role in popularizing the tropical house genre. He coined the term in 2013, and it has since become a recognized style in the music industry. Jack has also been credited with introducing Kygo to his former manager, Myles Shear, which has helped launch the careers of Kygo and Klingande.

Throughout his career, Jack has released several successful singles, including "Rivers," which peaked fourth on the Belgian chart, and "Rise Up," which peaked fourteenth in Belgium. His debut studio album was expected to be released in 2016, but its release date has not been confirmed. Jack has expressed his desire to continue creating music that pushes the boundaries of the tropical house genre, while also exploring new sounds and styles.

Despite his success, Jack remains humble and grounded, often expressing his concerns about being pigeonholed as a tropical house artist. He has stated that he wants to continue creating music that is true to himself, without being limited by the expectations of others. With his unique sound and infectious beats, Thomas Jack is sure to continue making waves in the music industry for years to come.

title: Patoranking
text:
Patoranking, born Patrick Nnaemeka Okorie on May 27, 1990, is a Nigerian Afrobeats and reggae-dancehall singer and songwriter. Growing up in the Ebute Metta community of Lagos, he shared a room with his parents and five siblings, which instilled in him a drive to create a better future. This upbringing, combined with his close relationship with his family, motivated him to pursue a career in music. 

Patoranking started his music career doing underground collaborations with artists such as XProject, Konga, Slam, and Reggie Rockstone. In 2010, he signed a record deal with K-Solo's Igberaga Records and released "Up in D Club" under the label. His breakthrough came in 2013 with the release of "Alubarika," a song featuring Timaya that opened doors for him in the music industry. The song's success led to him becoming a protégé of Dem Mama Records, although the exact nature of their relationship was later disputed.

In 2014, Patoranking signed a record deal with Foston Musik and released "Girlie O," a single produced by WizzyPro that put him in the limelight. The song's music video, shot and directed in London by Moe Musa, featured Patoranking liberating his next-door neighbor from domestic violence. A remix of "Girlie O" featuring Tiwa Savage was released to critical acclaim and debuted at No. 9 on MTV Base's Official Naija Top 10 chart.

Patoranking has released several successful singles, including "Daniella Whine" and "My Woman, My Everything," which charted on MTV Base Official Naija Top 10 chart. He has collaborated with other artists, such as Seyi Shay on "Murda" and Stonebwoy on the remix of "Pull Up." In 2015, he announced a distribution deal with VP Records, further expanding his reach.

Patoranking's music is a fusion of dancehall and Afrobeats, with lyrics that reference socio-political issues. He has cited Buju Banton, Bob Marley, Fela Kuti, and Lucky Dube as his key musical influences. In 2020, he released an album titled "Three" and announced a new album, "World Best," in 2023.

In his personal life, Patoranking maintains a quiet lifestyle. He has dated several high-profile individuals, including Ghanaian Television personality Joselyn Dumas and Nigerian singer Yemi Alade. He welcomed his first child, Wilmer Okorie, with businesswoman Leila Stone in August 2018 and has a second child, Welda Okorie. Patoranking's managers, Rickie Davies for International and Chimdinma Maduforo for Africa, handle his career affairs.

title: Ziaur Rahman
text:
Ziaur Rahman was a prominent figure in Bangladeshi history, serving as the sixth president of Bangladesh from 1977 until his assassination in 1981. Born on January 19, 1936, in Gabtali, Bogra District, Rahman came from a Bengali Muslim family. His father, Mansur Rahman, was a chemist, and his mother was Jahanara Khatun. Rahman had two younger brothers, Ahmed Kamal and Khalilur Rahman. He was raised in his home village of Bagbari and studied in Bogra Zilla School.

In 1947, Rahman moved to Karachi with his family after Pakistan gained independence. He attended the Academy School in Karachi and later joined the Pakistan Military Academy at Kakul. In 1955, Rahman was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Pakistan Army. He received commando training, became a paratrooper, and completed a special intelligence course. Rahman served in the Pakistan Army during the Second Kashmir War against the Indian Army, for which he was awarded the Hilal-e-Jurrat from the Pakistani government.

In 1971, Rahman played a crucial role in Bangladesh's independence war. He broadcast the Bangladeshi declaration of independence on March 27, 1971, from the Swadhin Bangla Betar Kendra radio station in Kalurghat, Chittagong, and was known as the "Announcer of the Liberation." Rahman was a prominent commander of the Bangladesh Forces and led the Z Force, a brigade consisting of the 1st, 3rd, and 8th East Bengali regiments.

After Bangladesh gained independence, Rahman became a brigade commander in the Bangladesh Army and later the Deputy Chief of Staff and then Chief of Staff of the Bangladesh Army. Following the assassination of President Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1975, Rahman was appointed as the Chief of Army Staff. However, he was removed from the position and put under house arrest after a coup in November 1975.

Rahman was freed in November 1975 after a mutiny staged by the Jatiyo Samajtantrik Dal (JSD) and a group of socialist military officers. He was reappointed as the Chief of Army Staff and became the chief martial law administrator. Rahman cracked down on the JSD and Gonobahini, and executed Abu Taher, a leader of the JSD, in 1976.

In 1977, Rahman became the president of Bangladesh and introduced massive reforms for the development of the country. He lifted martial law, reinstated multi-party politics, freedom of the press, free speech, and free markets. Rahman's government initiated efforts to create a regional group in South Asia, which later became SAARC in 1985. He improved Bangladesh's relations with the West and China and departed from Sheikh Mujib's close alignment with India.

During his presidency, Rahman faced numerous coup attempts, with at least 21 attempts reported. His government was also criticized for suppressing opposition, and at least 200 soldiers were executed by military tribunals. Rahman was assassinated on May 30, 1981, in an attempted coup in Chittagong.

Rahman's legacy is complex and divided in Bangladeshi politics. He is credited with ending the disorder of the final years of Sheikh Mujib's rule and establishing democracy by abolishing BAKSAL, the one-party rule established by Mujib. His economic reforms are also credited with rebuilding the economy. However, his critics argue that he suppressed opposition and was ruthless in his actions. Rahman's political party, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), remains a major force in Bangladeshi politics, and his widow, Khaleda Zia, has served as prime minister three times.

title: Guillermo Rigondeaux
text:
Guillermo Rigondeaux Ortiz is a Cuban professional boxer born on September 30, 1980. He is a two-time Olympic gold medalist and a seven-time Cuban national champion at bantamweight. Rigondeaux's amateur career was impressive, with a record of around 475 fights and 12 losses. He won gold medals in the bantamweight division at the 2000 and 2004 Summer Olympics, and also won several other international tournaments, including the World Championships and the Pan-American Games.

Rigondeaux turned professional in 2009, defecting from Cuba and signing with Arena Box-Promotion. He quickly made a name for himself with his fast hand speed, punching power, and exceptional defensive skills. He won his first professional fight on May 22, 2009, with a third-round technical knockout over Juan Noriega.

Rigondeaux's rise to prominence was swift, and he became a world champion in 2010, winning the interim WBA super bantamweight title. He went on to win the full WBA title in 2012, defeating Rico Ramos, and later unified the division with a victory over Nonito Donaire in 2013. Rigondeaux's win over Donaire was a unanimous decision, with all three judges scoring the fight in his favor.

Throughout his career, Rigondeaux has been known for his impressive skills and his ability to outmaneuver his opponents. He has been praised by boxing trainer Freddie Roach as being "probably the greatest talent I've ever seen." Rigondeaux has also been compared to other great defensive boxers, and is widely considered one of the best in the sport.

In addition to his victories over Donaire and Ramos, Rigondeaux has also defeated other top opponents, including Teon Kennedy, Roberto Marroquin, and Hisashi Amagasa. He has made several defenses of his titles, and has been involved in some closely contested fights throughout his career.

Rigondeaux has also had some notable experiences outside of the ring. He defected from Cuba in 2007, but initially attempted to return home before ultimately making his way to Miami in 2009. He has been open about his experiences as a defector, and has spoken about the challenges he faced in making the transition to professional boxing.

In 2020, Rigondeaux won the WBA (Regular) bantamweight title, and he held the title until 2021. Throughout his career, Rigondeaux has been known for his speed, power, and technical skill, and has established himself as one of the top boxers in the world.

title: Richard Burton
text:
Richard Walter Jenkins Jr., known professionally as Richard Burton, was a renowned Welsh actor born on November 10, 1925, in Pontrhydyfen, Glamorgan, Wales. He was the twelfth of thirteen children born to Richard Walter Jenkins Sr. and Edith Maude Jenkins. His early life was marked by tragedy when his mother died of postpartum infections when he was just two years old. He was subsequently raised by his elder sister Cecilia and her husband Elfed James.

Burton's interest in acting was nurtured from a young age, and he began performing in school plays. He was educated at Port Talbot Secondary School, where he developed a passion for reading poetry and English and Welsh literature. His schoolmaster, Philip Burton, played a significant role in his early life, providing him with intense tutoring and developing his acting voice. Burton eventually became Philip's legal ward and adopted his surname.

Burton's career began in the early 1940s, when he joined the Air Training Corps and performed in a radio adaptation of David Jones's epic poem "In Parenthesis." He was later discharged from the RAF and began his acting career in earnest, making his mainstream film debut in 1949 in "The Last Days of Dolwyn." He quickly established himself as a talented young actor, known for his mellifluous baritone voice and charismatic stage presence.

Throughout the 1950s, Burton appeared in a range of films, including "Now Barabbas," "The Woman with No Name," and "Waterfront." He also began to make a name for himself on stage, earning praise for his performances in plays such as "Adventure Story." In 1952, he was nominated for an Academy Award for his performance in "My Cousin Rachel," and he went on to receive multiple nominations for his subsequent films, including "The Robe," "Becket," and "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?"

Burton's personal life was also highly publicized, particularly his tumultuous relationship with actress Elizabeth Taylor, whom he married twice and divorced twice. He was known for his heavy drinking and his reputation as a great performer who had wasted his talent. Despite his personal struggles, Burton remained a respected and beloved figure in the entertainment industry, known for his incredible talent, his love of literature and poetry, and his iconic performances on stage and screen.

Throughout his career, Burton received numerous accolades, including a BAFTA Award, a Golden Globe Award, and a Grammy Award. He was also awarded a Tony Award for Best Actor in a Musical for his portrayal of King Arthur in the Lerner and Loewe musical "Camelot." Despite never winning an Academy Award, Burton was widely regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation, and his legacy continues to be celebrated by audiences around the world.

Burton's later years were marked by continued success, as well as personal struggles. He remained a top box-office star in the mid-1960s, earning fees of $1 million or more plus a share of the gross receipts. He continued to act in films and on stage, earning critical acclaim for his performances. Burton died on August 5, 1984, at the age of 58, leaving behind a legacy as one of the greatest actors of his generation.

In conclusion, Richard Burton was a highly acclaimed Welsh actor known for his incredible talent, his iconic performances on stage and screen, and his tumultuous personal life. Throughout his career, he received numerous accolades and was widely regarded as one of the finest actors of his generation. His legacy continues to be celebrated by audiences around the world.

title: Shaolin (humorist)
text:
Francisco Jozenilton Veloso, better known by his stage name Shaolin, was a Brazilian humorist, cartoonist, caricaturist, comedian, and media presenter. He was born on May 8, 1971, in Coremas, Paraíba. Shaolin began his career at the Teatro Municipal Severino Cabral in Campina Grande, where he likely developed his skills as a performer. He also worked as a presenter on Rádio Campina Grande and drew cartoons for several newspapers, including A Palavra, Jornal da Paraíba, and Revista Nordeste.

Shaolin gained popularity for his comedic work on various TV shows. His most notable shows include Domingão do Faustão, Show do Tom, and Tudo è Possível, where he would often satirize Brazilian celebrities, such as Leonardo, Joelma, and Zezé di Camargo. His humor and wit made him a well-known figure in Brazilian entertainment.

Tragedy struck Shaolin's life on January 19, 2011, when he was involved in a serious traffic accident on the highway BR-230 in Campina Grande. His car collided with a truck, leaving him with severe injuries. He spent several months in a coma, and even after being discharged from the hospital, he was still recovering from his injuries. In September 2012, Shaolin began to communicate again, using a machine that helped him by moving his eyelid.

In his personal life, Shaolin was married to Laudiceia Veloso, and they had two children together. Despite his accident and subsequent health struggles, Shaolin continued to be active on social media, with a Twitter account and an IMDb page.

Sadly, Shaolin's life was cut short when he passed away on January 14, 2016, due to a myocardial infarction. His death was a shock to his fans and the Brazilian entertainment industry, which had come to appreciate his humor and talent. Throughout his career, Shaolin left a lasting impact on Brazilian comedy and media, and his legacy continues to be remembered by his fans.

title: Jessie Mae Brown Beavers
text:
Jessie Mae Brown Beavers was a prominent American journalist and community leader in Los Angeles, California. Born on March 18, 1923, in Los Angeles, she was the daughter of Arnetta Hoyt Brown, a Baptist deaconess. Beavers earned a bachelor's degree in sociology from the University of California, Los Angeles. In 1947, she married insurance executive Leroy A. Beavers, Jr., and the couple had three children. Actress Dorothy Dandridge was one of her bridesmaids at their wedding.

Beavers began her career in journalism in 1944 as the editor of the family section of the California Eagle, a position she held until 1949. She then joined the staff of the Los Angeles Sentinel, where she worked as an editor until her death in 1989. In 1966, she was one of the organizers and leaders of the Los Angeles chapter of the National Association of Media Women. Her work in journalism earned her the Outstanding Woman in Journalism Award from the University of Southern California chapter of Theta Sigma Phi in 1969.

In addition to her work in journalism, Beavers was also a dedicated public servant. In 1973, she was appointed to the Los Angeles Human Relations Commission by Mayor Tom Bradley, a position she held for 16 years. During her tenure on the commission, she worked closely with fellow commissioner Toshiko S. Yoshida and chaired the affirmative action subcommittee. Beavers also organized hearings on racial bias in the entertainment industry in 1982. Her commitment to public service also led to her appointment to the Los Angeles County Music and Performing Arts Commission.

Beavers received several awards and honors for her work in journalism and community service. In 1968, she was cited for her work by the President's Youth Council. In 1972, she was honored by the Committee of Women for Good Government, alongside notable figures such as Quincy Jones and columnist Gertrude Gipson. In 1973, her colleagues and admirers, including Mayor Bradley and judge Vaino Spencer, hosted a tribute event in her honor at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel.

Tragedy struck Beavers in 1979 when she was assaulted and robbed in the driveway of her home. Despite this, she continued to be active in her community until her death on September 6, 1989, at the age of 66. Beavers is buried at Forest Lawn Cemetery in Glendale, California, and her legacy as a pioneering journalist and dedicated public servant continues to be celebrated. Her papers and photographs are preserved in various archives, including the Los Angeles Times Photographic Archives and the Oviatt Library at California State University, Northridge.

title: Ahmed Mumin Warfa
text:
Ahmed Mumin Warfa was a Somali scientist who specialized in botany and made significant contributions to his field. Born in Somalia, Warfa went on to become a professor at the Somali National University, where he taught biology and agriculture. His research focused on the flora of Somalia, and he collaborated with colleagues to discover several endemic species, including the Cyclamen somalense, which he discovered with his colleague Mats Thulin.

Warfa's academic career was interrupted by the civil war that broke out in Somalia in 1991. The war led to the closure of the university, and Warfa was forced to seek refuge elsewhere. He became involved in peacekeeping efforts, working as a translator for the United Nations and helping to set up councils for the reconciliation process in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. However, his efforts to bring peace to Somalia put him at odds with local militia leaders, and he narrowly escaped an assassination attempt in 1994.

Following the turmoil in Somalia, Warfa left the country and emigrated to the United States via Kenya. He continued to work in education, teaching biology at Salt Lake Community College and Brigham Young University in Utah. He also remained active in the Somali diaspora community, working as a reconciliator for the UN and the Somali President, and raising funds for projects such as Hiiraan University.

In 2020, Warfa returned to Somalia to take up the position of rector at the Zamzam University of Science and Technology. Tragically, his time in this role was cut short when he died of complications from COVID-19 on March 15, 2021, in Mogadishu. Warfa's legacy extends beyond his academic contributions, as he worked tirelessly to promote peace and education in Somalia. He is survived by his 12 children, who are a testament to his personal life and accomplishments. Throughout his career, Warfa demonstrated a commitment to his country and his field, and his passing is a loss to the scientific community and Somalia.

title: Lennie Hayton
text:
Lennie Hayton was a renowned American musician, composer, conductor, and arranger, known for his iconic captain's hat worn at a rakish angle. Born on February 14, 1908, in New York City to a Jewish family, Hayton developed a passion for music at a young age. He began playing the piano at six and attended many concerts with his parents, who, despite not being trained musicians, fostered his interest in music. However, they disapproved of jazz, which Hayton discovered in his teenage years.

Hayton's music career began when he joined the Broadway Hotel Orchestra as a pianist, led by Cass Hagen, a friend from his boyhood. In 1928, he was engaged by Paul Whiteman as a second pianist, playing piano and celeste, and acting as a part-time arranger. During his time with Whiteman, Hayton played with notable musicians such as Frankie Trumbauer, Bix Beiderbecke, and Bing Crosby. When Whiteman's orchestra downsized in 1930, Hayton joined the Charles Previn Orchestra, which had a weekly radio assignment.

In 1932, Hayton reunited with Bing Crosby, who had achieved significant success in music, radio, and film. Hayton provided musical support to Crosby on his theater appearances and radio shows, and they began recording together. Their collaborations included hits like "Cabin in the Cotton," "Love Me Tonight," and "Brother, Can You Spare a Dime?" which topped the charts. In 1933, Hayton became the musical director for the Chesterfield radio series "Music That Satisfies," featuring Crosby.

Hayton's work in Hollywood began in 1933 as the musical director for Crosby's film Going Hollywood, a Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer production. This marked the start of his successful career in Hollywood, where he worked on numerous films, including musicals starring Judy Garland. Hayton's work with MGM earned him four Oscar nominations, and he won the Academy Award for music for On the Town in 1950, sharing the award with Roger Edens. He also arranged music for Singin' in the Rain and received nominations for Star! and Hello, Dolly!, his second Oscar coming in 1969.

In addition to his work in film, Hayton composed and arranged music for various artists, including Frank Sinatra, and collaborated with other musicians on pieces like "Apple Blossoms" and "Stardust." Hayton's personal life was marked by his marriage to Lena Horne, whom he met while working at MGM. The couple's interracial marriage was tumultuous, and they eventually separated in the 1960s. Hayton, a heavy drinker and smoker, died of a heart attack in Palm Springs, California, in 1971, at the age of 63. He was buried in the Hollywood Forever Cemetery. Throughout his career, Hayton worked with many prominent musicians and contributed to some of the most iconic films and recordings of his time.

title: Dewi Sartika
text:
Dewi Sartika was a pioneering advocate for women's education in Indonesia, born on December 4, 1884, in Cicalengka to Sundanese noble parents, R. Rangga Somanagara and R. A. Rajapermas. As a child, she showed an interest in teaching, often pretending to be a teacher while playing with her friends. After her father's death, she lived with her uncle, who provided her with an education in Sundanese culture, while she also learned about Western culture from the wife of a resident assistant. In 1899, she moved to Bandung, a move that would set the stage for her future endeavors.

In 1904, Dewi Sartika founded the first school for women in the Dutch East Indies, named Sakola Istri, which was initially located at a corner of Bandung Regency's Pendopo. The school later relocated and changed its name to Sakola Kaoetamaan Isteri, or School of Excellence for Women, in 1910. The school aimed to provide education to women, and by 1912, there were nine schools with the same name in cities and regencies in West Java. By 1920, every city and regency in West Java had one of these schools, a testament to Dewi Sartika's vision and perseverance. In 1929, the school's name was changed to Sakola Raden Dewi.

In her personal life, Dewi Sartika married Raden Kanduruan Agah Soeriawinata, a teacher at Sakola Karang Pamulang, in 1906. However, her life was cut short when she died on September 11, 1947, in Cineam, Tasikmalaya, while evacuating from Bandung due to the independence war. Her grave was later moved to Makam Para Boepati Bandung.

Dewi Sartika's contributions to education and women's empowerment have been recognized and celebrated. She was awarded the Order of Orange-Nassau for her service in education and was honored as a National Hero of Indonesia in 1966. Her legacy continues to inspire, with streets and schools named after her, and a Google Doodle celebrating her 132nd birthday in 2016. Her pioneering work in education has left a lasting impact on Indonesia, and her name is synonymous with the fight for women's education and empowerment. Throughout her life, Dewi Sartika remained committed to her vision of providing education to women, and her achievements continue to inspire future generations.

title: Rachel Bilson
text:
Rachel Bilson is an American actress born on August 25, 1981, in Los Angeles to a show-business family.
